sentences.html: MANG AND MUSTARD
Roya Publication No. 26
by Chew Z
They gave him three cups, and he drank all three, and
lay down as one dead; and for seven days the living sat
about his body, keeping the fire, keeping the count — for
a soul can travel only as far as its body is guarded.
— of the rite of the mang, as an old man told it
SYNOPSIS
Majnoon, 1984.

In the flooded marshes of the Iran–Iraq war, nineteen-year-old Sohrab works the decontamination line of a field hospital — the first pair of hands the war offers its gassed, and the last many of them ever feel.
He keeps the ledger of the antidote: the small green-sleeved needles, counted like bread, that swing the poisoned back toward life.
Then the count stops balancing.

Twelve needles, missing in ones and twos, lead him not to the black market he expects but to a secret congregation of gassed survivors in an empty supply tent — soldiers who have discovered what Goshtasp, the old Zoroastrian who washes the dead, already knows: that the antidote is close kin to mang, the sacred drug an ancient rite once used, with three cups and seven days of witnesses, to send a righteous man to visit the dead.
In overdose, the medicine becomes a door.
On the far side wait the drowned and the burned, twenty years old forever, asking the questions the living have agreed not to ask.

And beyond the wire lies the marsh itself — five thousand years of reed houses and buffalo roads and guest houses that never refused anyone — being drained, burned and dyked out of existence by two armies arguing over a line.

As the crossings grow, the doses climb, and the war presents its bill in the bodies of strangers who were only standing where it was being held, Sohrab — keeper of the count, doorkeeper of the door — must decide what the drug truly is, what grief truly wants, and who keeps the vigil for a country.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with a coincidence I have not been able to leave alone.
The medicine used against nerve gas — pushed by the crate into poisoned conscripts during the Iran–Iraq war — is drawn from the nightshades, the poison-flowers, the same family of plants as henbane.

And henbane is a leading candidate for mang, the sacred narcotic of one of the oldest afterlife accounts in world literature: the Ardā Wirāz Nāmag, in which a righteous man drinks three cups, lies seven days while his sisters and the priests keep vigil over his body, tours heaven and hell, and returns to report what he saw.
The war’s mercy and the old religion’s door to the dead are, at the root, kin.
No one planned this.
Chemistry does not read scripture.
But I have come to think the coincidence points at something true: that every technology we build for surviving death sits closer than we like to the technologies we build for visiting it.
The historical ground of this book is real, and I have tried to keep faith with it.

Iraq’s chemical attacks on Iranian soldiers and civilians — the garlic smell, the laughter in the latency, the blindness arriving hours behind the wound, the tens of thousands still coughing decades later — are matters of documented record and survivor testimony, and the details in these pages stay inside what that record supports.
The people are invented.
The war is not.

Eight years, a million gone by some countings, and the border at the end where it stood at the beginning: if war has ever offered a cleaner proof that it needs no reason, only permission, I have not found it.

What interested me most, in the end, was not the crossing but the vigil — the old rite’s insistence that the traveler is nothing and the witnesses are everything, that a soul can only go as far as its body is guarded.

Grief, I have come to believe, is an ended conversation that the body refuses to file as ended, and every culture’s rites — the stone, the anniversary, the name said at the year’s turn — are attempts to finish the sentence.
This book asks what happens when a war manufactures unfinished sentences by the hundred thousand, strips away every vigil, and mass-produces the fuel.
The dead in these pages are not wise.

They are twenty years old forever, and they ask the questions of the naive and childish mind that destroys itself — whose water is this, where is a war kept when it is won, who says the sentence that ends it.
I do not answer them.
I do not think the questions have answers.
I think they have keepers, and this book is about what it costs to become one.

The marshes in these pages are the Mesopotamian marshes — the Ahwar — where the Tigris and the Euphrates run together, historically some fifteen to twenty thousand square kilometres of reed bed and lake, and by most reckonings the largest wetland in western Eurasia.

The Ma’dan who lived there built reed houses to a design that appears unchanged in Sumerian carvings five thousand years old, herded buffalo, wove mats, and kept a guest house in every village where no traveller was refused and no payment was ever taken.
Then the war used the marsh as a front line, because marsh stops armour and there was oil beneath it.
Afterward, and especially after 1991, it was drained on purpose: by the end of the century something like ninety per cent of it was salt crust, and the people were in camps in three countries.

In 2003 locals broke the embankments themselves and let the water back; there was a real recovery, and a UNESCO listing in 2016; and then upstream dams and a run of drought years pushed it down again, with heavy rains in early 2026 bringing a fragile, partial revival that nobody there is willing to call safe.
I have set Sohrab’s last chapter in 1993, at the bottom of it, because that is where he would have been standing, and because I did not want to hand the reader a recovery he could not yet have seen.
What I wanted to say about it is what a boatman says in the book: that nobody hated the marsh, and that this is the whole horror rather than any consolation.
Cruelty at least requires attention.
What happened there required only that a very large number of people, for eight years, not look at what they were standing on.

I. THE WARD
ONE. WASHING DAY

The trucks came up the causeway with their lights off, because lights drew the helicopters, and so the first Sohrab ever knew of a load was the sound of it: tires on wet gravel, and then the particular silence of men who have stopped screaming somewhere back along the road because screaming is a strength and the strength is gone.
He was nineteen.
He had been on the washing line four months, which at Majnoon in the spring of 1984 made him a veteran of the only trade he would ever fully learn.
The trade was this: the poison that fell on the marshes did not stay on the marshes.
It stayed on the men.

It lived in their clothes for days, in their hair, in the sweat-creases of their necks, patient as a debt, and it would burn the hands of any medic who touched them unwashed, and so before the doctors could have them, Sohrab had them.
Scissors, hose, bleach solution mixed in a drum until his eyes ran, a wooden table with a slight tilt so the water found the drain.
He was the first pair of hands the war offered its ruined, and the last pair many of them ever felt.
By the fourth month he had learned that the bodies came in three kinds, and he had names for each, and he told the names to no one.
The burned came first, usually, because the burned could sometimes still walk.
Mustard men.

The gas they had breathed and worn smelled, everyone said, like garlic, and the smell came off their uniforms so thickly at the cutting table that for the rest of his life the smell of a kitchen would close Sohrab’s throat.
Their skin did not look burned the way fire burns.
It lifted.
It came away in sheets, like wet paper coaxed from a wall, and beneath it the new surface wept.

The blisters rose wherever skin had touched skin — armpits, groin, the soft insides of elbows, wherever a man had sweated — great soft domes of amber fluid, some the size of a fist, that had to be moved around and never against, because the fluid, the doctors said, could mark whatever it touched.
Their eyes swelled shut so completely that some faces arrived without features, a smoothness where a face had been, and still the smoothness spoke.
It asked, politely, for water.
It apologized, more than once, for the smell.

One boy, his lids sealed to shining slits, asked Sohrab whether his eyebrows were still there, because his mother, he said, had always liked his eyebrows, and Sohrab said yes, they’re there, and it was true, and it was the only true comfort he gave anyone that week.
The second kind he called, privately, the drowned-in-air.
These were the nerve-gas men, and they frightened him far more than the burned, because there was nothing to wash.
They came off the trucks without a mark — no blister, no blood, boots laced, buttons done — dead the way sleeping men are dead in the first second you look at them, before you see the chest move.
Their chests did not move.

Their faces were wet, as if they had been weeping, and their mouths were wet, and when he thumbed back an eyelid, as he had been taught to do, the pupil at the center of the eye had shrunk to a point, a full stop, the smallest thing he had ever been asked to look at.
Some still held things.
A rifle.
A folded square of bread.

One held a green plastic canteen cap, only the cap, gripped so firmly that Sohrab left it with him, because prying open a dead boy’s fingers over a bottle cap was a thing he found, that morning, he could not add to himself.

The third kind was the ordinary, and it said something about the season that shrapnel and drowning and fire had become the ordinary, the almost restful — wounds that behaved like wounds, deaths with a shape he had grown up understanding.
Steel does what steel does.
Fire, at least, announces itself.
The clothing went into the pit.

That was the iron rule of the line: everything cut away went into the pit at the far edge of the compound, downwind, because a jacket could hold enough of the poison to blind the man who slept on it a week later.
The pit was the truest map of the month anyone kept.
Sohrab could stand at its edge and read the fighting in it — the sudden strata of a bad night, a layer of boys’ sizes from the day a volunteer unit had walked into the wrong reach of the marsh.
Nobody was assigned to count the boots.
There was a pile of them, by the pit, unpaired, and it grew, and everyone walked past it with their eyes managed carefully elsewhere, because a boot pile does an arithmetic that no one asks it to do.
His hands, by April, were their own casualty.

The bleach solution ate the skin of his knuckles until they cracked and wept a thin honest fluid of their own, and Goshtasp, the old man who kept the cold room, seeing them, brought him a tin of tallow without a word and without a word went away again.

On the last washing day of that month a truck came up the causeway carrying sixteen men, and Sohrab stood at the head of the line waiting for it in the grey before dawn, and he found that he could tell, from fifty meters, in bad light, by nothing more than the way each body lay against the boards and the tailgate — the burned rigid and apart from each other, guarding their skins even asleep; the drowned-in-air loose, spilled, at terrible ease — which of his three kinds each man was, and roughly what the next hour of his own life would be.
He was nineteen, and he understood, watching the truck grow larger, that this was the whole of the education the war intended for him, and that he was becoming excellent at it.
TWO. THE GARLIC RAIN

The shells that morning made a sound the men had not heard before — soft, almost apologetic, a cough instead of a shout — and where they burst, out along the forward reach where the Third Company was dug into the reeds, there rose not smoke exactly but a haze, low and unhurried, that smelled of garlic.
That is in the record.

Men five meters from a burst and men thirty meters from a burst reported the same two things afterward, in the same order: the smell of garlic, and a bitter taste at the back of the mouth, as if they had bitten a stem.
And they laughed.
This, too, is in the record, though the record gives it one line and the line deserves a book.
They laughed because nothing hurt.
Because the terror of gas, drilled into them for months, had promised claws, and what arrived instead was a kitchen.
The Iraqis have bombed us with perfume, someone shouted down the line, and the line laughed, and men waved their caps at the haze to hurry it along.
One man, a farmer’s son from near Shiraz, knelt at the edge of a flooded ditch, washed the itch from his face with marsh water, and ate his lunch with wet hands.
They all ate lunch.
The haze thinned.
The morning had been survived, and survival, in the fourth year of the war, was the entire syllabus; nobody had taught them that the poison’s first weapon was time.
By mid-afternoon the eyes began.
An itching first, blamed on smoke, on sleeplessness, on the marsh itself, which bred flies and rot and had made men’s eyes water since February.
Then a rawness in the throat, a voice going to gravel halfway through a sentence.
By dusk, men were shading their eyes from a sun that had already set.

By full dark the forward aid post was sending them back in threes and fours, each man’s hand on the shoulder of the man ahead, and by midnight the ward had become a thing Dr. Bijan would never afterward describe to anyone, because the description required saying that it was full of men going blind in the dark, screaming when the lamplight touched them, while skin that had been clean at noon rose, as the staff watched, into blisters — the flesh keeping its own delayed appointment, hours behind the injury, an ambush arranged that morning by a chemist years dead in another country.
The sergeant came in at two.
Both eyes were already gone under the swelling; he steered by voices.
When Bijan took his wrist to count the pulse the sergeant’s other hand came across and closed on the doctor’s sleeve with the exact grip of a man catching a rail on a stairway, and he said: Doctor.
Be honest with me.
It was nothing.
We laughed at it.
I stood in it and laughed.
A smell can’t be a wound.
Tell me a smell can’t be a wound.
Bijan was forty-one years old.

He had trained in Tehran and for two years in Manchester; he had come south in the first winter of the war for reasons he had stopped being able to reconstruct; and he knew, holding that wrist, the following things: that the sergeant’s lungs were already burned, because the gravel in the voice said so; that the blistering would worsen for another two days, because it always did; that the worst of the breathing lay perhaps sixty hours out; and that no treatment he possessed would do more than clean and cover and wait.
He knew also that it was two in the morning, and that the truth has a dosage like everything else, and that at this hour, in this ward, the full dose was lethal to no purpose.
“Rest now,” he said.
“The laughing did no harm.”
It was the sentence he would hate for the rest of his life — not because it was false, though it was false, but because it was skillful.
He heard the skill in his own voice, the smoothness of the thousandth repetition, and understood that the war had made him fluent in a language he had never consented to learn.
What was breaking Bijan was not the dying.
He had inventoried himself on this point with a clinician’s coldness and was sure of it.
Dying he had been trained for; dying had a curriculum.

What was breaking him was the interval — the specific cruelty of a weapon that let a man laugh, and eat lunch, and write a letter, and wash his face, for six or ten or fourteen hours, while the wound worked through him in silence, so that the doctor became the one who knew, the sole custodian of each man’s next three days, standing at bedsides in the position of a God he did not believe in and would not have forgiven if he had.
He had stopped washing his own face in warm water; he could not any longer say why, only that his hands refused it.
He had caught himself, twice, smelling his food before he ate, like an animal, and both times had gone on smelling it.
And he kept a tally now, in the back of the drug ledger where the columns ran out — not of the dead, which the war counted without his help, but of the lies.
A vertical stroke for each one, days ruled off with a line.
He told himself it was a discipline of honesty, a man keeping sight of what the work was costing.
On the bad nights the strokes ran to forty, and he understood the tally was not a discipline.
It was the truest triage log the ward possessed.

Because triage — the sorting of the wounded, the science of who is seen first, which he had learned as a clean triple fork: the ones who will live regardless, the ones who will die regardless, and the ones in between, for whom medicine exists — triage assumed that the sorted would hold still.
Mustard dissolved the categories while you watched.

Every man in the ward walked in as the middle kind and then migrated, hour by hour, in whichever direction his lungs decided, and the sorting had to be done again at dawn, and again at noon, a harvest that would not stay reaped.
So Bijan had abandoned the fork.
He triaged now by a single question, and the question was not who is worst.
It was who is changing fastest.

He went down the rows not looking at wounds but at rates — the interval between breaths shortening, a voice worse than an hour ago, a blister field advancing across a chest like weather on a map — and he learned the ugliest lesson the method had to teach, which was that it ordered him to walk past the quiet ones.
In an ordinary ward, quiet is recovery.
In this ward, quiet was the sign he had been taught to fear most, and the men with breath enough to scream were, by that very screaming, the ones who could wait.

Near dawn he stood at the door with his tally and heard the ward behind him — the coughing that would be worse tomorrow, the boy asking again about his eyebrows, the sergeant breathing in gravel — and he thought: they laughed at it.
And then, because he was honest in the ledger if nowhere else: so would I have.
It smelled of a kitchen.
Every one of us is built to walk toward that smell.
THREE. THE OLD MAN OF THE COLD ROOM
Goshtasp had washed the dead for forty years, and he had long ago stopped asking them to be explicable.

In the village where he learned the work, above Yazd, in the dry hills where his people had kept the old religion through thirteen centuries of other people’s patience running out, washing the dead had been a rite with rules older than the house it was done in — who might touch the body, and how, and what was said over the water.
Here it was a hose and a volume problem.
He did not complain about this.
A river does not complain about its banks.

He had come south with a nephew in the first year of the war; the nephew was under the ground at Khorramshahr; Goshtasp had stayed, because the war was producing the dead faster than it was producing men willing to be unafraid of them, and he was old, and unafraid, and there is a dignity in being the right man for a terrible job that the young mistake for sadness.
He thought of himself, privately, in the language of his grandfather’s trade on the river ferries: not as a holy man, which he was not, but as a man who knew a crossing.
Where the water ran shallow.
What it took.
What it left on the banks.
Death, watched daily for forty years without flinching, becomes a river like any other — never safe, never once safe, but known.
He watched the living too.
That was the part nobody assigned him.
The cold room had a doorway, and the doorway faced the recovery rows, and an old man on a stool in a doorway is furniture; men will do anything in front of furniture.

He had watched the young orderly, Sohrab, for four months now, the way one watches an apprentice who does not know he is one — watched him learn the three kinds without being taught, watched him leave the canteen cap in the dead boy’s hand, watched the bleach eat his knuckles and the boy say nothing.
The boy kept counts.
Not just the counts he was ordered to keep.
Goshtasp had seen him pause at the boot pile and refuse it with his eyes, which is itself a way of counting.
A ledger-keeping soul.
Such men, in Goshtasp’s experience, were the ones a crossing eventually found.
It was a Tuesday when he heard the man in the recovery row talking to the chair.
Not talking at the chair, as the fevered do, scattering words.
Talking to it — leaving the gaps a conversation leaves, listening into the gaps, answering what the gaps said back.

He was one of the gassed from the forward reach, a sergeant, a nerve case who had lived: they had put the antidote into his thigh twice on the causeway and once again at the door, and now he sat propped in the row with his skin flushed and hot and dry as a stone in the sun, his pupils blown wide and black — the antidote’s signature, the doctors said, the medicine swinging the body’s pendulum hard the other way — and his hands rose now and then to pick small careful nothings out of the air, and he was speaking to the empty chair beside his cot with a tenderness that made the men in the neighboring cots turn away in embarrassment, as from something indecent.
“You always do this,” the man said to the chair.
“You always let me win the argument and then you die again.
Stay and lose it properly this time.
I’ll make the tea.”
The orderlies looked away.
The doctor on rounds noted the delirium in his margin and moved on, because delirium was a known station on the antidote’s road and the road, for this one, led back to living.
Goshtasp did not look away.
He sat in his doorway with his hands folded and he listened, and what moved in him was not pity.
It was recognition — sixty years deep, sudden as a smell.
He had heard men talk to the unseen in exactly this register once before.
Not the fevered, not the mad.

Old men of his grandfather’s faith, in the hills, in a house with a fire that was never allowed out, men who had drunk something on purpose, with witnesses, and lain down as if dead, and spoken afterward — and once, dreadfully, during — in just this tone: tender, reasonable, mid-conversation.
A tone that does not describe the dead.
A tone that addresses them.
There was a word for what those men had drunk.
His grandfather had said it rarely, and always in the way one names a tool kept locked: respectfully, and without appetite.
Goshtasp sat in his doorway and tried the word silently first, like a key eased into a lock to learn whether it still fit anything.
Mang.
The flushed man laughed at something the chair had said.
Out along the causeway a truck was coming in with its lights off.

The old man looked at the antidote case standing open on the trestle by the ward door — the rows of little needles in their green sleeves, counted every shift, guarded like bread — and then at the sergeant, and then at the chair, and he decided, with the unhurried certainty of a man who has spent his life deciding when a body is ready, that the young ledger-keeper had earned the word, and would need it.
He rose from the stool, and went to find Sohrab, and said it aloud.
FOUR. THE OWNERS OF THE WATER
The army had learned, expensively, that no map of the marsh survives contact with the marsh.
Channels close in a season.
A reed bed that was open water in March is a wall in June.

So they hired men who carried the map behind their eyes, and one of them was Jabbar, son of Nasir, of the Hoveyzeh reeds, who was perhaps fifty and looked older and poled a boat the way other men breathe.
Sohrab drew him for a dawn run to the forward aid post — six ampoule cases and a sack of dressings, out and back before the light was high enough to interest anybody’s artillery.
He had expected to sit in silence.

Instead the old boatman, seeing a passenger who did not give orders, began to talk, and what he talked about was the country they were crossing, which Sohrab had been living in for four months and had never once seen.
The boat itself was the first correction.
Sohrab had assumed it was an army boat.

It was a mashoof — reed-built and sealed with bitumen, black, long, so light that Jabbar carried it on his head at the portages; a design, he said, that had not changed in any way anyone could name since before there were countries to change it.
His grandfather’s had been the same shape.
So had his grandfather’s grandfather’s.

There were pictures of it, Jabbar said, cut in stone in museums, made by people who had died four thousand years before the Prophet was born, and the pictures showed this boat, this exact boat, being poled by a man standing exactly here.
“You have to understand what this was,” he said, meaning the water they were moving over, and he said it without heat, as a man corrects a child’s arithmetic.
“You see a swamp.
A place where an army gets stuck.
I grew up in a city, boy.
It just had no streets.”
He gave it to Sohrab in pieces across an hour of poling.
The houses were made of reed and nothing else — no nail, no plank, no wire.
Qasab, the giant reed, grew four and five meters and higher, cut and bundled and set in facing rows and bent over and lashed, so the roof became a series of arches.

Sohrab, who had seen the inside of exactly one mosque worth the name, was made to understand that a big one had the proportions of a cathedral, ribbed like something’s ribs, the light coming down between the bundles in bars.
Built in a day.
Built by the village, in a day, without a single measurement taken, because the men’s hands held the measurements.
And when a family moved, the house was untied and poled away, or left, and the water took it back within a season and there was no ruin — nothing at all to say that anyone had lived there.
Nothing to excavate.

That detail lodged in Sohrab and would not leave: five thousand years of continuous habitation and almost no rubbish, because everything they used had been alive the year before and would be mud the year after.
The ground was made too, where it was needed.

An island of packed reed, kibasha, could be built in a week; layered with mud and rebuilt across generations it became dibin, real ground, and a man might live his life on land his great-grandfather had woven.
“We did not find places to live,” Jabbar said.
“We made them, and if we were wrong about where, we made them somewhere else.”
The buffalo cut the roads.
That was the part Sohrab made him repeat.

In the low-water season the herds were driven through the reed beds, and where they walked the reeds broke down, and the break became a channel, and the channel stayed open as long as boats kept using it — so that every road in the marsh was a road the animals had made and the traffic maintained, and a road nobody used for two years ceased to exist.
There was no authority anywhere in it.
There was no engineer.
The map was a habit held in common by people and animals, revised continuously, written down nowhere.
And the water was the wealth.
Not a hazard around the wealth; the wealth itself.
Fish so thick in the spring that a boy speared supper on his way home from an errand.

Wildfowl in numbers that darkened the light twice a year on the migrations, geese and duck and cranes coming down the whole length of the world and stopping here because here was where the world put the water.
Reed for the houses, reed for the mats the women wove and sold in the towns, reed for fodder, reed for fuel dried into cakes with the buffalo dung.
Rice where the land came up in season.
Buffalo milk, thick as paint.
Bitumen from the ground for the boats.
“A man could be born, married, and buried,” Jabbar said, “and every single thing that touched him in his life had come out of the water within one hour of his house.
Try to say that about your city, boy.”
Sohrab asked, because he was a ledger-keeper and could not help it, who had owned it.
Jabbar poled for a while before answering, and when he did he was amused rather than offended, which was worse.
“There were sheikhs.
There were tribes, and tribes fought, and I will not pretend to you that it was a garden of saints — a man could be killed in a dispute here the same as anywhere.
But own the water?” He shook his head.
“The fish were where the fish were.

The water came in the spring from the snow in mountains I have never seen, in a country I have never been to, and it went out again, and it did not consult us, and it belonged to nobody in the way that no one owns the wind.
You could own a buffalo.
You could own a boat.

Where I grew up, if you asked whose water this is, a serious man would have thought you were asking a riddle, and then he would have fed you and given you somewhere to sleep and waited three days before asking why a person with such questions had come.”
That, he said, was the law.
The mudhif — the guest house of a village, reed-built like the rest but on the grand scale, the sheikh’s, and belonging in practice to everyone — took in whoever arrived.
Anyone.

No traveler was ever refused and no payment was ever taken, not once, not from anybody, in a place where people had very little; and the taking of payment would have been a scandal remembered for a generation.

And in the boats, the courtesies ran the other way from every road Sohrab had ever walked: the man on the water greets the man on the shore first, and the man going downstream greets the man coming up, because the one with the current at his back is the one with breath to spare.
“You should have seen my grandfather’s mudhif full,” Jabbar said.
“Everyone inside it, and every single one of them wrong about something, and all of it settled by talking until it was settled.
That was the government.
Anyone who had walked in off the water had the right to sit in it.”
They were nearly at the aid post.

Ahead, the causeway the army had bulldozed through the reeds two years before ran out across the water like a stitch through a lip, and beyond it the pontoon bridges, and beyond those the smell of the war.
Sohrab sat with the ampoule cases between his knees and did an accounting he did not enjoy.
Five thousand years.
No paper.

No deeds, no titles, no surveys, no registry, no borders, no fences, not one line drawn on anything — a whole civilization run on habit and hospitality and the memory of where the buffalo had walked, held for fifty centuries by people who had never once needed to write any of it down.
And now two states, each of which could produce a document, were fighting over it with artillery.
“Do you understand what I am telling you, boy?” Jabbar said, leaning on the pole, not looking back.
“It is not that they came and took our water.
It is that they arrived with the idea that water is a thing that can be taken.
We had no argument prepared for that.
Nobody here had needed one in five thousand years.”
FIVE. THE MANG OF WISHTASP

They sat in the cold room after the last truck, because it was the one place no one entered willingly, and Goshtasp set the lamp on an empty trestle between them and told it the way a tired man tells a tired man — no scholarship, no sermon, one flame.
“Long before the Arabs came,” he said, “before the faith this army fights under was born, my people had a bad century.
Wars, and after the wars, doubt.
You understand doubt, boy — not the philosopher’s kind.
The kind that gets into a whole people at once, like damp into grain.
They had buried too many, and the question that was killing them was simple, and it is the same question being asked tonight in every trench in these marshes: is any of it true?
The bridge the soul must cross.
The scales.
The garden and the pit.
Or do we bury our sons into nothing.
“So the priests did a thing I have never stopped thinking about.
They did not preach.
They decided to send a man to look.
“They gathered at the fire temple — the great fire, the one that is never let out — and out of the whole community they chose the cleanest soul among them, a righteous man.
The books call him Wiraz.

And I will tell you the strangest small thing first, so you know I am not decorating: his seven sisters wept and argued against it, the way sisters argue, because they understood before anyone said it plainly that the journey might not return him.
They were overruled.
Even they, in the end, agreed to it.
That is how badly the living needed word from the dead.
“They prepared him the way we prepare a body — mark that, boy, the way we prepare a body.
He washed his head and his body.
He put on a new garment.
They perfumed him.
They spread clean bedding, and he lay down on it, and he ate a last meal, and he remembered the dead by name, the way one does at a funeral — his own funeral, held early, with him listening.

And then the priests filled three cups — the books say golden cups, but I have known books to gild things — three cups of wine mixed with the drug called mang, and he drank all three, and lay back, and was gone.
“Seven days.
Seven days and seven nights his body lay there breathing slow, and here is the part everyone forgets, and it is the whole story: the story is not about his soul.
Any fool can leave.
The story is about the ones who stayed.

Seven days his sisters and the priests sat around his body in a ring — keeping the fire fed, keeping the prayers going in shifts, keeping the flies from his face — because they held, as an article of the rite itself, that a soul can only travel as far as its body is guarded.
The vigil was not decoration around the miracle.
The vigil was the road home.
“And he crossed.

The books say a shining spirit met him and took his hand and led him to the bridge — the bridge every soul comes to, wide as a meadow for the good and narrow as a blade for the wicked — and he walked among the dead and saw everything.
He saw the rewarded.
He saw the punished, and mark this too: the punishments were not fires invented by a landlord.
Each punishment was only the deed itself, given back.
The man who had watered down milk for children stood ladling a milk that was never full.
What you did is what you get, forever, undiluted.
My grandfather said the pit is only a mirror with the mercy removed.

“Then, on the seventh day, his soul came back down the road his sisters had kept open, and entered his body, and he woke as if from a pleasant sleep, and asked for food, and then he told them everything, and a scribe wrote it down.
And people are reading his report tonight, boy, somewhere, twelve centuries later.
One man’s trip, taken so a whole people wouldn’t have to keep asking in the dark.”
The lamp fussed.
Sohrab said: “And the drug.
The mang.”
“The mang of Wishtasp, the old books call it, and I should tell you why, since you will want the name straight.
Wishtasp was the king — the first king to take the faith, the one the prophet himself is said to have convinced.
There is a story that he was the first to be given the draught, so that he could be shown what he was being asked to believe in before he asked a whole people to believe it.
So the drink carries his name the way a road carries the name of the man who first walked it.
When my grandfather said the mang of Wishtasp, he meant: this is not something a man brews for himself on a bad night.
This is the one that kings were given, in front of everybody.”
Then he turned his hands over, palms up, a man showing he hides nothing.
“And now I must be honest with you, because the honesty makes it worse and not better.
Nobody alive is certain what plant mang was.
The old books name the word and not the field it grew in.
The scholars quarrel — some say one herb, some another.
But the candidate my grandfather’s people held to, the one the old men in the hills held to, is the henbane.
The poison-flower.
Pale petals, dark veins, a smell like something sleeping badly.
It grows in ditches and graveyards, which the old people did not consider a coincidence.
A family of plants that kills in one measure and opens doors in another, and has never once agreed to tell anyone in advance which measure they have taken.”
He looked at the antidote case by the door — the little needles in their green sleeves, counted every shift.
“Your medicine, boy.
The one you push into the drowned-in-air to swing them back.
The doctors will tell you it is made from that same family of flowers.
The poison-flowers.
The nightshades — henbane among them.

The chemists went into the ditch where the old drug grew and came out holding the same stem, and they found the medicine inside the poison, which is a fine trick, and nobody thought to ask the flower what else it had been used for.
So understand what is standing open on that trestle every night, counted like bread.
The same family.
Perhaps the same door.

They found it before either of us was born, boy, and they used it carefully, three cups, seven days, a ring of witnesses — and we use it by the crate, on the causeway, in the dark, with no witnesses at all.”

Sohrab walked back along the recovery rows afterward, past the flushed boy sleeping now with his hands finally still, and he put it to himself in plain words, because plain words were how he kept his ledgers: the medicine we push into the gassed is close kin to a drug an old religion once used, carefully, with its whole community watching, to send a man to visit the dead — and we are spending it by the case, with no one watching at all.
He checked the count before he slept.
It balanced.
It was the last night it ever would.
INTERLUDE I. FIRST CROSSING
Minute one.

The needle is still in Morteza’s hand when the ward tips like a boat and pours him out of it, and the pouring does not hurt, and he is standing in the marsh — but the marsh is wrong in a way his body accepts before his mind can object: the water is perfectly still, and perfectly clear, and there is no smell.
The marsh has smelled of diesel and rot and garlic for three months.
Here the air is like the inside of a jar.
Minute two.
His cousin Yusef is sitting on the surface of the water, cross-legged, the way he used to sit on the flat roof at home, and he is sorting stones.
There is a heap of wet stones beside him and he is moving them, one at a time, to a second heap, and when the second heap is done he begins moving them back.
He does not look up.
He was drowned in February, off a speedboat, in the night assault; he is not wet.
Minute three.
“You came,” Yusef says, pleased, still sorting.
“Sit.
Mind the water, it belongs to somebody.”
“Whose is it?”
“That’s it.
That’s the question.” Yusef holds a stone up to the light that comes from nowhere.
“Whose water is this?
We were told it was ours under the world and theirs on top, or theirs under and ours on top, I forget the order.
Did they measure it before they filled it with us?
Somebody must have the paper.
You would know.
You keep papers now.”
Minute five.
Morteza tries to say I’m sorry and finds the words have no purchase here, they slide off the still air like water off wax, and Yusef watches them slide with mild interest.
“Don’t bring those,” he says.
“They don’t work.
Bring answers, if you come again.
I have a list.” He counts on his fingers, and his fingers are the fingers of the boy he was at nine, though the rest of him is twenty.
“One: whose water.
Two: the bread that came up on Thursdays — was that ours, or was it borrowed from the week after?
Because some weeks it tasted borrowed.
Three: when a war is won, where is it kept?
Is there a room?
Who has the key to the room?
I have thought about this one a long time.
Everything that is won is kept somewhere.
A cup.
A harvest.
Where will they keep this, when they win it?”
Minute nine.

Time here is a texture, not a line; Morteza understands that whole minutes are passing in the ward, that his heart out there is galloping and his skin is burning dry, and that here the light has not moved at all.
Yusef sorts his stones.
The heaps never grow and never shrink.
“Does it hurt,” Morteza asks.
“Being — this.”
Yusef considers it honestly, the way he considered everything, which is why he was the one everyone sent to settle bets.
“It doesn’t hurt,” he says.
“It weighs.
Thursdays are heavy.
I don’t remember the town anymore, but I remember it was heavy on Thursdays, and it is still heavy on Thursdays.
That’s what I kept.
You keep the strangest things.
Pack better than I did, when you come.”
Minute fourteen.

The light begins, at last, to move — which means the antidote is losing its grip out there, the pendulum swinging home — and Yusef looks up for the first time, and his face is exactly his face, and this is the worst moment, the exactness.
“You’ll come again,” he says.
It is not a request, and it is not a welcome.
He picks up the last stone and holds it out — and does not give it.
“Morteza.
Why do you keep coming to a place you aren’t finished with?”
Minute fifteen.

The marsh pours him back the way it poured him out, and the ward assembles itself around his cot piece by piece, canvas, lamplight, a man coughing three rows down, and his own heart hammering like something that has run all the way here to warn him, too late, about nothing that can be changed.
II. THE COUNT
SIX. TWELVE MISSING
The count was simple, which is why nobody wanted it.
Cases in, cases opened, needles used, needles remaining.
Each autoinjector logged against a casualty’s name or, when the casualties outran the names, against a tally mark and a time.

The ledger lived in a canvas satchel and the satchel lived on Sohrab’s shoulder, because four months ago a supply sergeant had looked down the line for the man least likely to be shot soon and least likely to lie, and had chosen the washing boy, and that was the entire ceremony of his appointment.
He was good at it the way he was good at everything the war gave him: without pride, with total attention.
He knew the arithmetic of the antidote the way a shepherd knows a flock at dusk, by silhouette, before counting.
Two needles to the causeway teams.
Six in the ward reserve.
A case of forty under the trestle, seals unbroken.
The numbers had a shape, and on the eighth of the month the shape was wrong before the addition was.
Twelve missing.
He did the count three times, then did it backward, then took the ledger out under the light and did it a fourth time with a straightedge under each line like a schoolboy.

Twelve needles, drawn across six days, in ones and twos — never enough in a single day to startle the eye, which told him at once that the taking was patient, and that the taker understood how counting men see.
He reported it to no one, that first night.
He wants to be able to say, later, that this was caution.
It was not caution.
It was the ledger-keeper’s private shame, the conviction that a missing number is first of all an accusation against the man who keeps the number.
Instead he thought it through the way the war had taught him to think, which was downhill, along the worn channels.
The front had a black market the way a body has a temperature.

Cigarettes moved, and dry socks, and morphine when there was morphine, and places on the leave rosters, and the antidote — the antidote was money in a way morphine could never be, because morphine only bought comfort and the needles bought tomorrow.
A man with two injectors taped inside his shirt walked into the gas with a different spine than the man beside him.
Everyone knew it.
There were officers rumored to carry four.
So: theft, for sale.
The ordinary war.
He found he was almost comforted by the theory, and noted the comfort in himself with distaste — that he would rather serve alongside a thief than inside a mystery.
He began to watch.
He varied the hours of his counts.

He learned to sit with Goshtasp in the cold-room doorway at dusk, because furniture sees everything, and for four evenings he saw nothing except the ordinary economy of exhausted men: bread moving, tobacco moving, a boot exchanged for a boot.

On the fifth evening he saw Morteza — the nerve case, the one who had lived, the one who had talked to the chair — walk to the trestle where the ward reserve stood, lift two needles in their green sleeves with the unhurried competence of a man taking what is his, and walk out along the duckboards toward the supply tents, into the dark, not once looking behind him.
A thief checks behind him.
Sohrab stood in the doorway a long moment, cold in a way the evening did not explain, adjusting the theory the way you adjust to a step that isn’t there.
Then he followed.
SEVEN. THE STATEMENTS

The order came down mid-month that an intake record was to be kept for the chemical cases — name, unit, distance from the burst, time of onset, the casualty’s own account in his own words — because somewhere far to the rear it had been understood that the world would one day ask for proof, and would ask for it in the voice of a notary.
The task fell to Sohrab, because he already held the ledger, and because the men trusted the washing boy in a way they did not trust anyone with rank.
He ruled each page into two columns.
The left column was the man’s words, taken down as spoken.
The right column was the clinical shorthand he had been taught: the abbreviations for blister and burn-percentage and breath-rate, the body’s own statement, entered opposite.
He did not choose the design for cruelty.
He chose it because paper was short.

But he understood, within a day, what he had built: a page on which what a man believed had happened to him and what had actually happened to him stood side by side, in the same ink, refusing to agree.
From the intake record, eighth through the nineteenth of the month:
— Private, 21, infantry.
Distance from burst: fifteen meters, perhaps twenty.
“There was a smell like garlic, strong, and a bitter taste in the mouth like biting a green stem.
We joked about it.
I want that written — that we joked, because no one told us, not because we were careless.
A few hours after, the dizziness, the headache, and by night I could not get air down past my throat.
My voice has been going and coming since.

Small blisters began on the neck and under the arms, then not small.” Right column: voice near-whisper; lids swollen, prized open for examination; blistering neck, axillae, groin; breath fast and shallow.
— Corporal, 26.
“I carried Hasan on my back from the reeds to the boats, eight kilometers by the dyke path, because his eyes had closed and he could not see the duckboards.
His jacket was soaked from the spray of the shell.
Nobody told me a wet jacket could burn the man carrying it.
I want it written that I would have carried him anyway.
Write that first, before the rest.” Right column: deep burns across the shoulders and back in the print of a jacket’s shoulders and back; the carried man admitted separately, alive.
— Volunteer, 17, attached as a runner.
Would not give a distance; kept saying he was fast.
“The smell was more like geraniums, I think, than garlic.
My grandmother grows them.

That is the last thing I could smell; since then, nothing, not even bleach, and the ward smells of nothing, and I know the ward cannot smell of nothing.” Right column: total loss of smell noted; eyes intact; lungs the concern; observation.
— Sergeant, 34.
“Write down that I got my mask on in time.
Write it in the record with my name spelled correctly.
My wife’s brother is in the Ministry; my wife reads everything.
I got it on in time.
The blisters are from the skin, from the sleeves, not from breathing.
A man can be burned through cloth and still have been careful.
Write: he was careful.” Right column, in Sohrab’s hand, after a long pause of the pen: burns consistent with exposure through clothing; mask time not verifiable; entered as stated.
— Private, 19.
Distance: five meters.

He talked for the whole examination, softly, a list of colors — the exact yellow of a dust road at evening, the blue a kettle turns, a green he had no name for that lives inside wet reeds when the sun is low.
He was cataloguing.
His lids were sealed shut and the doctors did not yet know what was underneath.
“If it comes back, it comes back,” he said.
“If it doesn’t, I want the colors written where somebody keeps them.” Sohrab wrote the colors.
Right column: both eyes — and then nothing, the shorthand refused, entered at last as: see over, and overleaf, in longhand, the colors again.
— Private, 23, of the flooded ditch, of the washed face, of the lunch eaten with wet hands.
“Tell me which it was.
The water or the air or the bread.
I need it to have been one thing.
A man can be angry at one thing.” Right column: exposure route indeterminate; multiple; and the shorthand for the lungs, worsening.
— Woman, age not given, of the reeds east of the pump channel.
Distance from burst: not given; she was cutting fodder.
Her account, through a soldier who had the Arabic: “We heard it and we went down into the boats and into the channel, low, in the shade, as one does.
My mother taught me and her mother taught her.
Nobody has ever come out to us to say the low place is the wrong place.

If somebody had come out and said one sentence to us, one sentence — do not go low — I would have four of them here instead of two.” Right column: burns to hands, forearms, face and scalp; both eyes; and beside it, entered because there was nowhere else to enter it, the number four.
— Boy, approximately nine.
Distance from burst: at home.
He would not speak to the doctors and spoke to Sohrab because Sohrab was washing him.
“Is it in the water now?
Because we have to drink the water.

My uncle says it goes away by itself and my brother says it stays in the reeds for years and one of them is lying to me and I need to know which one, because if it stays we cannot go back and nobody will tell me.” Right column, after a long pause of the pen: nerve exposure, dosed at 22:40; and in longhand, because the shorthand had no entry for it: told him honestly that I did not know.

— And on the nineteenth, at the bottom of a full page, a man whose name Sohrab copied twice to be sure, who dictated one sentence and turned his face away: “My mother is Khadijeh, daughter of Yusef, of the village above the salt river; say that I said her name while I could still say it, and say I said it looking at the person writing.” Right column: Sohrab looked at him while he wrote it, so that the record would be true, and then entered the breath-rate, which was the only other honest thing he had.

At night he read the ledger back, left column against right, the testimony against the body, and understood that he was keeping two histories of the same war and that they would never once agree — and that of the two, only the right column had never been afraid, never been proud, never protected a wife or flattered a ministry or begged a smell to come back.
The left column was men.
The right column was what the war was actually doing to them, written in the only language that has no dialect for hope.
He kept both.
That was the job.
He kept both.
EIGHT. THE CAUSEWAY
The intake record taught Sohrab what the poison did to men.

The causeway taught him what the war did to everything the men were standing on, and it taught him in the same way — slowly, with a latency, so that he had been looking at it for months before he understood he was looking at a wound.
It began with the roads.
An army cannot move on channels cut by buffalo, so the army made roads: earth dykes bulldozed straight across the reed beds, kilometers of them, packed and revetted and raised above the water.
They were magnificent, in their way.
They were also dams.

Water that had gone one way since the snow first came down out of the mountains now arrived at a wall, and stopped, and stood, and went stale — and on the far side of the wall the reed beds that had fed on that water for five thousand years discovered thirst inside a marsh, which Sohrab would not have believed possible and then saw with his own eyes: qasab going brown in standing water two hundred meters from a lake.
Then the channels.

Both armies cut them, for the boats and the amphibious craft, straight where nothing in the marsh had ever been straight, and the straightness pulled the water off in directions it had never gone, and drained places that had been wet since the Sumerians, and flooded places that had been dry enough to grow rice.
Then the fire.
Reed burns.
Reed hides men, so reed burns — kilometers of it, deliberately, to open fields of view, sending up a smoke Sohrab could see from the compound for a week and a smell that got into the laundry.

And in the black afterward, nothing: the reed beds were the country’s whole architecture, its walls and its fodder and its fuel and its cover for the birds, and where they burned there was open water with a scum on it and no shelter for anything.

Then the oil, from the wells and the pipelines and the tanks that had been hit, which came down the water in slicks the color of a bruise and put a skin on everything, so that the buffalo drank it and the reeds wore it and the fish came up dead in windrows along the dykes.

And then the mines, in the shallows, which did not care in the slightest whether the leg belonged to a soldier or a woman cutting fodder, and which would still be there — Sohrab understood this even in 1984, standing on a dyke with a case of ampoules — long after every man now alive in these marshes had gone home or been carried out.
He asked Jabbar about the birds, because of what he had said about the light darkening twice a year, and Jabbar said, “They come.
They are not stupid.
They circle, and they see what it is now, and most of them go on.
Where they go on to, God knows.
Perhaps there is nowhere.
They are old, boy, older than us, they have been coming down this way since before there was anybody here to watch them arrive, and they came for the water, and we have made the water into this.”
Jabbar’s village had been on a dibin — real ground, woven and mudded and rebuilt across four generations of his family — two hours by pole from where the compound now stood.

In the second year of the war a dyke went through half a kilometer to the north; in the third year the water on their side went first stale and then shallow and then salt, because that is what water does when it stops moving in a hot country; the rice failed; the buffalo, which cannot live without deep water to stand in and clean fodder to eat, began to die in a way Jabbar described once, flatly, and never again, and which Sohrab afterward wished he had not asked about.

In the winter the family went out to a camp on the edge of Ahvaz — a settlement of block houses and standpipes and a road, where his wife could not weave because there was no reed, and his sons could not fish because there was no water, and where an old woman of his household who had lived her entire life within sight of water and had never in eighty years been more than a few steps from a boat sat in a concrete room and, in Jabbar’s phrase, “began to forget in order.”
They had a house with a door that locked.
Jabbar said this the way a man reads out a strange number from a page: a door, with a lock.
There had never in his life been a lock in the marsh.
There had been the mudhif, which took anyone in.
And still he came back, every week, and poled the army’s medicine through his ruined country for a wage.
Sohrab asked him why, once, on the way back with the empty cases, and he expected one of two answers — money, or hatred — and got neither.
“Because the water is still there,” Jabbar said.
“Bad water.
Half of it.

But it is still there, and the day it is gone nobody will remember where the channels were, because the channels are not in any book, boy, they are in me and in perhaps forty other men and when we are finished they are finished.
So I go up and down.
I keep them open.” He shifted the pole.
“You keep your count.
I keep mine.”
Sohrab did not answer, because there was nothing to say to a man doing the same job as you with the far larger ledger.
They came in past the burnt beds at dusk.

Somewhere behind them a fresh dyke was being pushed out into the water by men who would be gone within four years, on a project no one would ever unbuild, cutting a line that would still be lying across that country when everyone in this boat was dead.
“They will say afterward that they had to,” Jabbar said.
“Their generals and their generals.
And they will be telling the truth, in the way that a man drowning another man is telling the truth when he says he needed to stand on something.”
NINE. THE SUPPLY TENT

The supply tents stood in a row at the western edge of the compound, and the last of them had been half-emptied in March and never restocked, and it was toward this one that Morteza walked, and Sohrab followed at the distance the dark allowed, along the duckboards, past the generator that gave every man in the compound the same excuse not to hear anything.
There was a lamp inside, turned low.
He could see it breathing against the canvas.
He stopped at the seam of the doorway, in the smell of mildewed webbing and marsh, and he did not go in, because what he heard from inside was not commerce.
It was the register.
The one from the recovery row.
The tenderness that made men look away.
He looked in.

Seven of them sat in a circle on crates and folded blankets — he knew five by name and all seven by their intakes, gassed men, survivors, the ward’s alumni — and in the circle’s center, on an ammunition box draped with someone’s prayer cloth, lay a single autoinjector in its green sleeve, and nobody was touching it.
That was the first thing that undid his theory entirely: twelve needles missing and one on the altar and no money anywhere, no goods, no scale-eyed men.
The needle was not being traded.
It was being attended.
Morteza added the two he carried to the box, unhurried, and sat, and for a while the circle only breathed.
Then a man Sohrab knew as Akbar, a machine-gunner with mustard scars like spilled wax down his left jaw, leaned forward and spoke — not to the circle.
Past it.
“Hasan.
It’s Thursday.
You said count the Thursdays, so I’m counting.
Fourteen.
Your mother had the stone set upright; my brother saw it and says the lettering is good, deep lettering, it will outlast the mason.
You asked me whose water it was.
I asked an engineer.
He laughed at me, Hasan.
I’m still asking.”
He sat back.
Silence took the tent again, hospitable, unembarrassed.

Then another man spoke into the middle distance, a message to a dead brother about a debt that was now paid, that he wanted it known was paid; then a boy no older than Sohrab, who said only, “Father, the thing you asked me in the reeds — I don’t have it yet.
Don’t ask me so early next time.
Let me sit down first,” as if grief were a visitor who kept arriving before the house was swept.
Sohrab understood, standing in the seam of the tent with his ledger strap cutting into his shoulder, what he was looking at.
It was a waiting room.

The needle on the cloth was not tonight’s ceremony; tonight was the vigil before it, the messages being gathered the way a traveler gathers letters from a village before walking to the city, because not everyone can make the trip, and the one who goes carries for the rest.
And he understood something else, which frightened him more, because it was administrative.
Seven men.
Twelve needles over six days.

One or two crossings a week, each witnessed by the others — witnessed; the word arrived in Goshtasp’s voice — rationed, recorded somewhere in somebody’s head with a care that matched his own ledger line for line.
It was not an outbreak.
It was an institution, already running, with dues and a waiting list and a doctrine of carrying letters, and it had grown up inside his count the way a root grows inside a wall.
Morteza looked up then, directly at the seam of the doorway, without surprise, and Sohrab knew that he had been seen for some time, perhaps from the trestle, perhaps for days.
“Come in, ledger-keeper,” Morteza said, gently, making room on the crate beside him.
“You of all people.
We’ve been keeping a count too.”
TEN. THE DOORKEEPER
They did not threaten him.

He had braced for it walking in — for the circle to close, for the oldest grammar of men caught at something — and instead they made him tea on a spirit stove and waited while he drank it, and the waiting was worse than threat, because it assumed him.
“You’ve done the arithmetic,” Morteza said.
“Twelve.
It will be thirteen by Friday, I won’t lie to you inside this tent; that’s the first rule here and you’ll hear it again.
So.
Say the accusation out loud, so it’s been said.”
“You’re stealing medicine,” Sohrab said.
“Each needle you take is subtracted from a gassed man on a stretcher who hasn’t arrived yet.
That’s the whole of it.
Everything else is decoration.”
“Everything else is decoration,” Akbar agreed, the scarred one, nodding slowly, as if Sohrab had recited the first line of a catechism correctly.
“That is exactly what it is.
Now ask us why seven men who have each been on that stretcher would do it anyway.”
He had no answer, so Morteza gave it to him plainly, the way the intake record had taught them all to speak.
The crossing was real or it was not — the tent held both opinions, peaceably, which surprised Sohrab more than anything else that night — but what it did was not in dispute among them.
A man went across, and sat with his dead, and finished something.
And came back quieter.
Not healed; nobody in the tent used the word healed; the tent’s word was settled, the way ground settles after rain.
“You wash the living,” Morteza said.
“The old man washes the dead.
There’s a third washing, ledger-keeper, for the part of a man that stands in the doorway between those two rooms and can’t enter either.
That’s what the needle is.
That’s all it is.”
“Then take your case to Dr. Bijan and ask for it honestly.”
The tent laughed, without unkindness, the way men laugh at a boy who has suggested writing to the king.
“The doctor would burn this tent by morning,” Akbar said, “and he would be right to, by everything his ledger measures.
We know what we’re stealing from.
We’ve decided the theft is owed.
You don’t have to agree.
You have to count.”
And there it was, the thing they had brought him in for, laid on the cloth beside the needle.
They did not want his silence; silence they had already had for weeks, and it had cost them nothing.
They wanted his ledger.
Keep the count, exactly, honestly, needle by needle — but keep it for the tent as well as against it.
Know who had crossed and when and on what dose.

Hold the line at which borrowing became butchery, because they did not trust themselves to see that line from inside their own need; they had watched need before, at the front, and knew what it did to men’s arithmetic.
“Every rite that ever worked had a man like you in it,” Morteza said.
“The one who stays sober.
The one who watches the body and the clock and the count while the others cross.
The old religion knew it — ask your old man, he’ll tell you.
The traveler is nothing.
The vigil is everything.
Be the vigil.”
“And if I refuse?
If I report it?”
“Then you report it,” Morteza said simply.
“No one here will touch you.
We’re not that kind of congregation.

But the needles will still go missing, ledger-keeper — from worse men than us, with no count at all, and no witnesses, and the first you’ll hear of it is a boy dead on a crate with no one watching his body, and you’ll know the number was loose in the world because you declined to hold it.”
Sohrab walked back along the duckboards past the generator, and the compound was the same compound, and the satchel on his shoulder weighed what it had always weighed, and everything was different.
He had come out expecting to feel like a man who had discovered a crime.

He felt instead like a man who had been read a will and found his own name in it — appointed, without consent, to an office that had existed for twelve centuries and had been standing vacant in this compound, waiting for whoever kept the count.
He did not report it that night.
He told himself he was deciding.
He was already keeping their ledger by Friday.
INTERLUDE II. SECOND CROSSING
Minute one.

The tent folds away like a page turning and Qorban — the farm boy, the youngest of the circle, who has waited five weeks for his turn — is standing in his father’s orchard, except the orchard is indoors somehow, the rows of trees running under a ceiling he can feel but not see, and the light is the color of late afternoon and does not move.
Minute two.

His father is halfway up a ladder that leans against nothing, picking fruit into an apron, and the fruit is not any fruit Qorban knows — pale, heavy-looking, without smell — and when the apron is full his father climbs down, empties it into a basket, and the basket, without drama, is empty again, and his father climbs back up.

He died of the coughing sickness two winters before the war, in his bed, in the ordinary way, and it is somehow shameful here, his ordinary death, among all these drowned and burned — a man who merely died, doing the work he merely did.
Minute three.
“You’re thin,” his father says from the ladder, not looking down.
“Did it rain in the spring?”
“It rained, Father.”
“Good.
And the harvest.
What was the harvest?”
Minute four.

Qorban begins to explain — that he was conscripted in the autumn, that his brother took the orchard, that there is a war, that he is in the marshes now, in the south, that the trees are safe, and his father listens the way he always listened, patiently, wholly, and then says:
“Yes.
But what was the harvest?
How many sacks?”
Minute six.
He does not know how many sacks.
He says the war again, and the word goes into the still air and his father turns it over the way he would turn a windfall fruit, checking for the bruise, and hands it back.
“I don’t know that measure,” his father says, without reproach.
“Is it more than a drought or less?
When it’s over, what fills the store-room?
Tell me in sacks, and I’ll understand it.”
Minute nine.
Qorban stands under the ladder and tries.

He tries to convert it — the marshes, the smell of garlic, Hasan’s stone with its deep lettering, the boot pile no one counts — into sacks, into anything a store-room could hold, and the arithmetic will not go, there is no rate of exchange, and his father waits with the full apron, kind, unhurried, holding out the one question the whole ladder of him has come down to ask, and the question cannot be made to fit anything Qorban has spent two years doing.
Minute eleven.
“The trees are safe,” Qorban says at last, which is true, and his father nods, satisfied, and empties the apron into the basket that will not fill.
“Then it was a good year,” his father says.
“Whatever else.
Write it in the book as a good year.” And then, pausing on the ladder, feeling upward for a fruit, his back to his son: “Qorban.
The thing you keep bringing me.
The war.
You carry it here like a harvest, every visit, and you set it down, and you wait for me to weigh it.
I have tried.
It doesn’t weigh.
It isn’t a thing that grew.
Why do you keep bringing it to a place where it doesn’t weigh?”
Minute twelve.

The orchard’s un-light flickers, which means the pendulum is coming back, and the last Qorban sees is the apron, full again, and the basket, empty again, forever, neither of them minding, and he surfaces on the crate in the supply tent with his pulse shouting and his mouth like a dry field and Sohrab’s hand on his wrist, counting, and the count in Sohrab’s face saying: back inside the line, this time, barely.
“Well?” Morteza asks softly, from the circle.
“It was a good year,” Qorban says, and begins, without any noise at all, to weep.
III. THE VIGIL
ELEVEN. WHAT MORTEZA BROUGHT BACK
It was Morteza who broke the tent’s own first rule, and he broke it carrying something true.

He came up out of a crossing on the last night of the month — a long one, near the line Sohrab had ruled in red, his pulse at the top of the bracket, his skin hot as a stove door — and before the water was in him, before he was properly behind his own eyes, he said: “Karim-of-the-mortars.
The one lost in February on the north spit.
He’s in the reed bank where the old pump channel bends.
West side of the bend, under the fallen section of walkway.
Yusef showed me.
He kept saying somebody should get the paper right.
He’s there.”
The tent went still in a new way.
Messages had come back before — questions, weights, Thursdays — but never a claim with coordinates.
Never a thing the living world could go and check.
They went and checked.

Akbar and two others, on the second night, with a lamp and a grapple, along the pump channel to the bend, and under the fallen walkway section, in the reed bank, west side, they found him — what the marsh had kept of him, four months’ worth, his tags legible, his paybook a green pulp in his breast pocket.
Karim-of-the-mortars, entered missing in February, struck from missing in June.
The paper made right.
For a day the tent walked half a meter off the ground.
Proof — the word moved among them like contraband.
The crossing was not a mercy or a madness; it was a road, and roads went to real places, and things could be carried back down them, and Karim was the receipt.

It was Sohrab, keeper of both ledgers, who took it to Bijan — not as confession, he told himself, but as a question wearing a report’s clothing: a body recovered on information from a delirious man; how would the doctor account for it?
And Bijan, who did not yet know about the tent and heard only a strange rumor of a dream, dismantled it without heat, in four sentences, the way he read an X-ray.
Morteza and Karim had served the same sector in February.
The fallen walkway was on the withdrawal route every survivor of the north spit had used; a hundred men had passed within twenty meters of that reed bank in the dark, in panic, half of them wading.
A man sees more than he knows he sees, the doctor said.
Panic writes it down and files it where waking can’t read, and delirium is a clerk with no respect for filing.
The drug didn’t take him anywhere.
It opened a drawer.
Every word of it was reasonable.
That was the trouble.

Sohrab carried the explanation back through the compound and felt it working exactly as far as explanations work and no further, because Bijan’s account and the tent’s account now stood side by side in his head like the two columns of his own intake ledger — the believed and the measured, refusing to agree, and both written in ink.
He put it to Goshtasp in the cold-room doorway, wanting the old man to rule, and Goshtasp declined the gavel with the mildness of a man who had watched this exact argument for sixty years.
“Of course there’s a plain explanation,” he said.
“There is always a plain explanation.
There was a plain explanation for Wiraz too — a man sleeps seven days, a man dreams what his priests need him to dream.
The books don’t record that anyone was converted by the report who wasn’t already kneeling.” He fed the lamp.
“You want one of the columns to win, boy.
That’s youth.
They don’t fight.
They just don’t visit each other.
You’ll keep both.
That’s the job.
You told me so yourself.”
In the tent, the needle count went up by two the following week — fourteen, in Sohrab’s hand, where there had been twelve.
Proof, it turned out, was the strongest dose of all, and it had entered the congregation’s bloodstream, and there was no antidote listed anywhere in the ledger for that.
TWELVE. THE ARITHMETIC OF MERCY

The shells came at dusk on a Friday, the soft coughing kind, out along the eastern reach where a replacement company had rotated in that same morning — men three days from home, who knew the drill from a lecture — and the trucks began arriving before full dark, and the war presented its invoice for everything the tent had borrowed.

Sohrab was on the line, scissors and hose, when the runner came from the ward shouting for the reserve case, and he heard, through canvas and forty meters, the exact moment the count betrayed itself: Bijan’s voice, flat and carrying, saying not thirty-one; count it again; the case holds forty, we have logged nine, count it again — and then the runner’s silence, which was itself the recount, and then Bijan’s voice again, one register lower, ordering the doses stretched.
Stretched.
The arithmetic of mercy, done aloud, in front of everyone.

The drowned-in-air on the stretchers needed the antidote in a rhythm — the medicine wore off faster than the poison did, so a man had to be dosed and dosed again, the pendulum held by force until his own body could hold it — and a rhythm cannot be stretched without silences, and each silence had a man inside it.

The doctors went down the rows making the choice the missing needles had already made for them, and the choosing had a sound, and Sohrab stood at the washing table with a boy’s ruined jacket in his shears and listened to it, and could not make his hands move.
One man died in the gap.
That was the number, when the night finally balanced.

A conscript from the replacement company, gassed in his third day of war, who was dosed once, and held, and needed the second needle at the turn of the hour, and the second needle was nine minutes finding him, because the reserve was thin and the thin was being rationed, and nine minutes was longer than he had.
Perhaps he dies anyway.

Bijan said so, unasked, in the doorway of the ward at dawn, to no one, in the voice of a man testing whether a sentence can bear weight: heavy exposure; he was late to us; perhaps he dies with the full case on the trestle.
Perhaps.
The word did no work.

Everyone within hearing knew the count was short, though only one man in the compound knew where the shortage had gone, and he was standing at the washing table with his knuckles bleeding into the bleach, discovering what the tent’s word settled cost at market.
He did not sleep.

He sat in the cold-room doorway through the morning with the satchel on his knees, and did the whole ledger again from the first page, the licit column and the hidden one, and when Goshtasp brought him tea he said, without preamble: “His name was Davud.
I washed him myself.
Nineteen.
My age to the season.” And then, because the old man only waited: “The tent bought its dead a visit and paid with a stranger.
And I kept the account that made it possible, and I ruled a red line for their pulses and none for this, because I never believed the bill would arrive while I was holding the book.”
“And now you’ll go to the doctor,” Goshtasp said.
It was not quite a question.
“Now I’ll go to the tent,” Sohrab said.
“The doctor gets the truth when I understand what it is.
The tent gets it tonight, whole, with Davud’s name in it, and they can sit in their circle and carry that message for once — the living have questions too.
Let them answer one.” He stood, and the satchel swung to his shoulder with its familiar, intolerable weight.
“And then either the crossings end, or the tent finds fourteen needles’ worth of another way, or I burn it down myself and count the ashes.
Those are the columns now.
There’s no third one.”
He was wrong about that, as it happened.
There was a third column, and it had his own name at the head of it, and it was already ruled, and had been since a Tuesday in the spring when an old man said a word to him across a lamp.
But the ledger does not show a man his own line.
That is the one mercy ledgers keep.
THIRTEEN. THE ONES WHO WERE ALREADY HERE

They came in at four in the afternoon in two mashoofs and a commandeered fishing boat, and the first thing that was wrong was that they came in quietly, and the second thing that was wrong was that some of them were small.

The shells had gone long, or had gone exactly where they were sent; nobody in the compound would ever know which, and Sohrab noticed within the hour that everyone had independently stopped asking, which was itself a kind of answer.

Wherever they went, they went into a stretch of half-drained marsh eleven kilometers east where four families had stayed on because the water there had not yet turned and because a man does not leave a place his great-grandfather wove out of reeds simply because artillery is landing four kilometers away; that arithmetic had been running in his favor for two years.
Nineteen of them.

Sohrab counted, because counting was the first thing his hands did in the presence of a load, and he was still counting when he understood that the count included a woman of about sixty and three children.
They had no masks.
That was the entire tactical situation, stated.
A soldier has a mask and a drill and a whistle signal and a sergeant screaming at him; he may fail all of it, and often does, but the system exists and he stands inside it.

A woman cutting fodder at the water’s edge with a child on the bank behind her has none of it — has, in fact, nothing but a smell of garlic on the wind and whatever she happens to know, which is nothing, because nobody had ever come out to these reeds and explained to anybody what to do when the air turns.
Worse: they had run the wrong way.
Sohrab pieced this together at the cutting table from three separate accounts and had to stop working for a moment when it resolved.
The gas was heavy; it sank; it pooled in the low places and ran along the ground like water finding a level.

And the people of that marsh, on hearing shellfire, had done what five thousand years of instruction told them to do, which was to get low and get into the boats and get down among the reeds — into the ditches, the channels, the shaded cuts, the exact low sheltered places where the stuff was lying thickest.
Their own competence had killed them.
The knowledge that had kept that family alive on that water for four hundred years had, in the space of ten minutes, been converted into a set of instructions for dying.
The washing line took them the way it took everyone.

But the clothes were wrong in his hands, and the smallness was wrong, and there was an old woman whose hair had to be cut away who kept apologizing to him in an Arabic he half understood, apologizing, for the trouble, for the water, for taking up his afternoon, and
Goshtasp came out of the cold room and worked beside him for four hours without being asked and without speaking a word.
Nine of the nineteen were nerve cases.

Bijan did the count in the ward doorway with the reserve case open in front of him and the runner standing there and no expression whatever on his face, and Sohrab, arriving with the ledger because the ledger was what he was for, watched a man arrive at a subtraction he had already done in his head twice and hoped to be wrong about.
The reserve was thin.
It had been thin since the eighth of the month.

Nine nerve cases needed dosing and re-dosing on a rhythm — the medicine wearing off faster than the poison, the pendulum held by force until the body could hold it alone — and on the causeway there were also, that same evening, two batteries’ worth of men in positions that had been shelled forty minutes earlier and might be shelled again before midnight, and the standing instruction on the distribution of the antidote existed and was unambiguous and had been written in a building none of them had ever seen.
Sohrab heard the doctor say, quite calmly, to the runner: “Combat first.
That is the order.
I am not appealing it tonight.” And then, after the runner had gone, to nobody, in a different voice: “Ask me what the order is for.
Go on.
Ask me what a front is for, if not for the people standing on it.”
They stretched the doses.
