Everyone in the ward that night knew exactly what stretching meant, because they had learned it three weeks earlier on a boy called Davud, and Sohrab moved up and down the rows with the case and the ledger and entered the times, and the times were the whole story: this one at 21:10, this one at 21:52, this one — a boy of perhaps nine, whose distance from the burst was entered in the record as at home — at 22:40, which was nineteen minutes late, and who was still alive at dawn, and who was one of the ones who lived, and Sohrab never learned whether the nineteen minutes had cost him anything permanent, because the survivors went out on a truck to Ahvaz on the third day and the compound had no mechanism whatsoever for finding out what became of a civilian.
Six of the nineteen died in the compound.
He washed all six.
And under all of it, running the whole night like a second ledger he could not close, was the arithmetic he had no right to be doing and did anyway.
Sixteen, now.

Twelve by the eighth of the month and four more since, because proof had raised the appetite the way proof does — sixteen needles, taken in ones and twos, spent on crossings, on messages carried to the drowned, on Thursdays counted for a man under a stone with good deep lettering.
He had kept that count himself, in his own hand, in a book nobody else could read.
Sixteen would not have covered nineteen.
Sixteen would not have covered nine.
But sixteen was not nothing, and nine was not nothing, and somewhere between those two facts was a space exactly the size of a boy of nine at 22:40, and Sohrab stood in it for the rest of his life.
He said none of this to the tent.
He said it, at four in the morning, to Goshtasp, who was rinsing his forearms at the trestle, and who listened to all of it and then said the only thing that was true:
“They had no mudhif here, boy.
Nowhere to send their message, nowhere to sit, nobody to sit with them.

That woman has been on this water longer than either of our peoples have had a name for it, and she will be entered tonight in your book as an unnamed civilian, female, approximately sixty.” He shook the water off his hands.
“Your tent has stolen sixteen needles to finish their conversations.
Nobody in this compound has stolen so much as a lamp to finish hers.”
FOURTEEN. THE QUARREL OF THE TWO PRIESTS

He went to the tent and said Davud’s name into the circle, and the circle took it the way ground takes rain — no defense, no flinch, Morteza only nodding slowly and saying, we’ll carry it, which enraged Sohrab more than argument would have, and he walked out before the rage could spend itself where it wasn’t owed.
The debt was older than the tent.

He took it to the cold room, where the oldest creditor in the compound sat trimming a lamp, and he put the satchel down between them like a body, and the two of them talked from full dark to first light, and what follows is that night, which the compound never knew occurred, and which decided everything that came after.
“Tell me what it actually does,” Sohrab said.
“Not the story.
The story is beautiful and Davud is dead.

Tell me what the drug does, old man, in plain words, because I have kept every count in this compound honestly except the one that matters: I have never once written down what it is we are actually buying.”
Goshtasp trimmed the lamp and let the question sit until it had stopped vibrating.
“Then let us do it as a washing,” he said.
“Plainly.
Piece by piece.
What does the drug do.
First, the body — you know the body better than I do, you’ve held the pulses.
It dries a man and heats him and swings his heart up like a run uphill.
It takes the eyes’ aim away.
And somewhere past the second needle, it takes the doorman.”
“The doorman.”
“The one in a man’s head who stands at the door and says: that is real, come in — that is not, wait outside.
Every waking hour of your life he’s on duty, boy, unthanked.
Fever bribes him.
Exhaustion distracts him.
This drug walks him off his post entirely.
And then everything in the courtyard comes indoors at once — memory, wish, grief, the dead — and none of it is wearing a badge, and the man inside greets it all as guests.
That is the delirium.
I have watched it for forty years from this stool.
It is not a window, and it is not a lie.
It is a house with the doors taken off.”
“Then it’s nothing,” Sohrab said.
“Then Bijan is right and the whole tent is men talking to their own furniture, and Davud died for furniture.”
“Slower,” Goshtasp said, without heat.
“You keep two columns; keep them now.
I said what the drug does.
I have not yet said what the visit does.
They are not the same entry.” He set the lamp between them, deliberately, the little fire of the rite in miniature.
“Answer me something first, ledger-keeper.
Why do the living want to talk to the dead?
Not these living.
All of them.
Every people we have a record of, boy — every one — has built something for it.
Graves close to the house.
Stones with the name cut deep so the thumb can read it when the eyes blur.
Food set out at the year’s turn.
Prayers with the dead’s names threaded in.
Photographs now.
Letters written to men who will never collect them; I have seen three in this compound, folded into breast pockets, addressed.
Why?
The dead ask for none of it.”
“Comfort.”
“Comfort is a word people use to stop looking.
Look longer.
A death, boy — especially a death like this war makes them, sudden, far off, mid-sentence — a death is a conversation ended by the other party without consent.
Everything unsaid at that moment stays unsaid, and unsaid things do not dissolve.
They lodge.
You’ve seen where they lodge; you wash it every day.
The shoulders.
The breath.
The hands that keep doing a task the task no longer needs.
Grief is not a feeling, whatever the songs say.
Grief is unfinished business held in the body, and the body has no procedure for finishing it, because the procedure requires two parties and one is gone.
So every people that ever buried anyone has built what I would call finishing-rooms — the grave, the stone, the anniversary, the prayer.
Places where the living can conduct their half of the ended conversation with enough ceremony around it that the body is persuaded, a little, that business is being transacted.
That the sentence got its ending after all.
Every funeral you have ever attended was a message sent to a closed door, on the theory that the sending is the cure.
And it half is, boy.
It half is.
That is the tragedy of the whole apparatus.
It half works.”
“And the mang finishes what the funeral half-does.”
“The mang,” Goshtasp said, “opens the finishing-room and puts a chair in it, and the chair answers back.
That is its entire power, and you should be exactly as frightened of it as you are, because nothing in the history of grief has ever answered back before.
The stone doesn’t.
The photograph doesn’t.
The prayer doesn’t — don’t tell the mullahs I said so.
A man stands at all of them and does both voices himself, and knows he is doing both voices, and that knowing is the splinter in every rite we’ve ever built.
The drug takes out the splinter.

In that house with no doors, the dead arrive wearing their own faces, speaking in their own cadence — you’ve heard the men; the cadence is perfect, it is the one thing delirium never gets wrong, because it was recorded by love, and love is a meticulous clerk.
And the man says what he could not say, and hears — something — say back what he needed said.
The sentence ends.
The business transacts.
And the body believes it, boy.
That is the whole medicine.
Not the vision.
The body’s belief that the accounts are settled at last.
You have seen them come up out of it.
You have the pulses written down.
Tell me what you see in the week after, and be honest, because I know what I see.”
Sohrab was quiet a long time.
“They sleep,” he said at last, grudging as a confession.
“Akbar stopped the thing he did with his jaw.
Qorban eats.
The shaking ones shake less.
It’s in my margins — I didn’t rule a column for it, but it’s in my margins.”
“It’s in your margins,” Goshtasp agreed.
“Settled, they call it.
Ground after rain.
Forty years of washing what grief does to the living, boy, and I have never seen anything settle men like this settles them.
There is my column.
Now give me yours.
You’ve been building it all night; I can hear it.
Spend it.”
And Sohrab spent it — everything he had entered against the tent in four weeks of keeping its ledger, the case for the poison with good manners.

That the drug does not open a door; it dims the room until the mind, desperate and tender, furnishes it, and the furnishing is made entirely of the mourner himself, so the dead say nothing the living did not carry in — Yusef’s questions are Morteza’s questions, wearing a loved voice; the orchard’s sacks are Qorban’s own untranslatable war handed back to him.
That the perfection of the cadence proves the opposite of what the tent thinks it proves: it is exactly as perfect as memory, and no more, a recording, not a residence.

That what the visits produce is not settlement but rehearsal — the men return calmer not because the wound has closed but because they have found a room where the wound is permitted to stay open forever, tended, furnished, visited on Thursdays; and a wound with visiting hours does not heal, it institutionalizes.

That the doses climb — his own red brackets, month on month, drifting upward like water finding its level — because a finished conversation stays finished, but a rehearsed one has to be rehearsed again, and again, which is the signature of the poison and never of the cure.

And that the whole account was now notarized by a dead conscript from a replacement company, because a room like that is paid for in the currency of the room next door, where men needed the pendulum held and the hands holding it were short sixteen needles.
“It numbs and it loosens, both at once — that is all it does,” he finished.
“It numbs the doorman and looses the furniture.
Everything else is what we pour into it.
And I have watched what men pour, old man, and it is bottomless, and the case on the trestle is not.”
The lamp had burned to its knuckle.
Goshtasp did not answer at once, and when he did, he did the thing Sohrab had least prepared for: he agreed.
“Yes,” he said.
“All of it.
The room is furnished by the mourner.
The dead speak in borrowed cadence with nothing of their own to say.
The dose climbs.
The settlement may be rehearsal wearing settlement’s coat.
Yes, boy.
Do you imagine the old ones didn’t know?
Do you think twelve centuries of priests never noticed what you noticed in a month with a straightedge?” He leaned forward, and the last of the lamp stood in his eyes.
“Why do you suppose the rite was built the way it was built?
Three cups, measured by another’s hand — never the traveler’s own.
Once — Wiraz crossed once, boy, once for a whole people, not every Thursday.
The traveler chosen by the community, not self-selected by the size of his wound.
And around the body, for every hour of seven days: witnesses.
Sisters.
Priests.
The fire kept.
The count kept.
You asked me once why the vigil, if the soul does the traveling.
Now you have earned the answer.
The vigil is not protection for the journey.
The vigil is the protection from the journey.

The witnesses are there to hold the border the drug erases — to be the doorman the traveler has drunk away, to say to him with their hands and their prayers and their patience: this far, this once, this dose, and back.
The crossing was never trusted to the crosser, because the old ones knew exactly what you know: that grief’s appetite is bottomless and the door only opens inward.
The vigil is the technology, boy.
The drug is only the fuel.
And what this war has done — what your tent has done, with its beautiful manners and its rationed needles — is strip the vigil and mass-produce the fuel.”
He sat back.
Outside, the first trucks of the morning were coming up the causeway with their lights off.
“So you are both right, you and the tent, and neither of you will win, because the columns don’t fight; they don’t visit.
The drug is a door and it is a poison with good manners; it was always both; that is why it was locked, not thrown away.
The sin isn’t the drinking.” He took the satchel from between them and set it back on Sohrab’s shoulder himself, an investiture, and his hands were very steady.
“The sin is drinking unwatched.
And if you ever drink, boy — and I see it in your ledger-keeping, I have seen it since Tuesday in the spring, you will — you come to me first.
A body deserves a witness.
Even yours.”
FIFTEEN. THE CONFISCATION
The political officer arrived on a Sunday, which the tent would later agree it should have read as an omen, since nothing administrative had ever before happened to the compound on a Sunday.
He was young, younger than Bijan, with the clean boots of the rear and a folder he never opened, because the folder was a prop and the information was already in him.
Someone had talked.
It did not matter who; in a compound of exhausted men it never matters who; a secret held by nine people is a message with a slow fuse.
He convened no tribunal.

He simply appeared in the supply tent at dusk with four military policemen and had them carry out the crates, the blankets, the prayer cloth, the spirit stove — the furniture of the finishing-room, itemized aloud as contraband, stolen medical stores, and unauthorized assembly — and the words he used interested Sohrab even through the fear, because nowhere among them was the word that mattered.
Not drug.
Not delirium.
The State’s vocabulary walked all the way around the thing itself and never looked at it.
The charge, when it was read to Morteza in the headquarters tent, was defeatism.
Sohrab, summoned as the keeper of the stores ledger, stood at the canvas wall and understood, listening, what the army was actually afraid of, and it was not the theft.
It was the messages.
“You tell men,” the political officer said to Morteza, not angrily, in the reasonable voice of a man adjusting a machine, “that their dead ask questions.
Whose water is this.
Where is a war kept when it is won.
You understand that a soldier who has heard his dead brother ask what the war is for returns to the line as a rifle that has been asked what it is for.
An army is men who have agreed not to ask each other that.
You have built, in a supply tent, with government needles, a place where the asking is holy.” He tapped the unopened folder once.
“If you had been selling the antidote, Sergeant, you would be in less trouble.
A thief subtracts needles.
You subtract the agreement.”
Sohrab did ask one question, from the canvas wall, and regretted it for years afterward, not because of the answer but because of how quickly it came.
He asked whether the intake record should continue to carry the civilian entries — the woman of the reeds, the boy dosed at 22:40 — or whether those belonged in some other file.
The political officer glanced up as though a chair had spoken.
“Those are not casualties of the unit,” he said, already looking back down.
“Enter them as local persons present in the area of operations.” Present in the area of operations.
Five thousand years, and the State had a phrase for it, and the phrase was four words long and put them in the category of weather.

Morteza said only one thing in his own defense, and Sohrab wrote it in the hidden ledger that night, word for word, because it was the tent’s entire theology in a sentence: “The questions were already in the men, Captain.
We only gave them somewhere to be asked.
A question with nowhere to be asked doesn’t die.
It digs.”
They took him west the next morning, to what the paperwork called a rest facility, with a stop first, the escort said, at a place where doctors would help him with his confusion.

The tent’s remaining members were dispersed along the line into separate companies with the tidy instinct of a man scattering coals so the fire will die politely — and made, thereby, into carriers; within a month Sohrab would hear the tent’s exact liturgy, the Thursdays, the letters carried across, described to him by a stranger from a unit twelve kilometers north, the way one hears one’s own dialect in a foreign city.
The needle count, in the weeks after, balanced perfectly.
Sohrab reported the balance up the line and was commended for it.
And every evening he sat in the cold-room doorway with the satchel on his knees and felt the balanced ledger for what it was: not order restored, but a room emptied.
The men still went by on the duckboards with their unfinished sentences lodged in their shoulders.
The finishing-room was confiscated.
The grief was not.

It had merely lost its address, and Sohrab, who now held the only working key to the only remaining door, sat with the key in his lap each evening, and each evening it was heavier, and he began — he could feel it happening, entry by entry, the way the missing twelve had first announced themselves — to keep a small private count of his own reasons for not using it, and to notice the count was falling.
INTERLUDE III. THIRD CROSSING
From the hidden ledger, the last shared vigil, the night before the Sunday.
Three crossings, witnessed.
What was brought back, as dictated to the keeper.
Akbar’s, minutes four through seven.
Hasan is repairing a net.
The net has no tear that Akbar can find, and Hasan repairs it anyway, contented, the shuttle moving like speech.
“I counted your Thursdays,” Akbar tells him.
“Fourteen more.” — “Good,” Hasan says.
“Somebody should hold the numbers.
They took mine when I came here; you can’t bring numbers across, they’re too heavy; it’s why nobody here knows the date.” He works the shuttle.
Then: “Akbar.
In the reeds that night, when the water lit up — I have been meaning to ask someone who would know.
Who paid for the electricity?
Wire costs money.
Current costs money.
Somebody signed a paper so the water could do that to us.
I don’t want his name.
I want to know what the paper said.
Papers have to say something.
What could it have said?” Minute seven: the net is whole and he mends it.
The net is whole and he mends it.
Qorban’s, minutes three through nine.
Not the orchard this time.

His father stands at the store-room door with the ledger of harvests open, the family’s true scripture, forty years of sacks in columns, and he is trying to enter something and the pen will not make the mark.
“Your war,” he explains, apologetic.
“I promised you I’d weigh it.
I have been trying since your last visit.

Look —” and he shows the page, and the page holds every year of Qorban’s life in his father’s careful hand, and where this year should be there is a smoothness, the paper refusing, like water refusing a nail.
“Everything that ever happened to this family fit in the book,” his father says, and he is not sad, he is puzzled, which is worse.
“Droughts fit.
The flood fit.
Your grandfather’s death fit — one line, but it fit.
What have they made out there that doesn’t fit in a book, Qorban?
And why are they making so much of it?”
The third was the boy whose father died in the reeds, the one who asked to sit down first.
His crossing, the keeper’s note says, was quiet for eleven minutes and he would dictate only the ending.

His father and he sat on the fallen walkway above the pump channel, feet over the clear water, and far down in the water there were lights, and he asked his father what the lights were and his father said: those are the ones still arriving; the marsh brings them down slowly, it is gentle that way, gentler than the boats.

And then his father took his hand — the note records that the boy’s actual hand, on the crate, in the tent, closed at this minute, grip strong, duration a full minute, witnessed by all — and said: “You’re cold.
You were always cold in the spring, even little.
Listen.
They will tell you it will be over by the year’s turn.
They told us the same, and the ones before us the same.
Sit with me and we’ll watch who’s winning from here.
You can see it very well from here.

Look.” And the boy looked, and the water was clear all the way down, and there was nothing to see but the arriving lights, and his father said, gently, as if delivering the news the whole marsh had asked him to pass along: “That’s it.
That’s the whole view.
Now say it slowly, what I taught you, so I know you have it before you go back up.” — “Who is winning?” the boy said slowly.
And his father nodded the way he had nodded over schoolwork done right, and let go of his hand, and the tent’s lamp came back on all at once like a held breath let out.

The keeper’s final entry for the night records only the doses, the pulses, the durations, and then, in a different pen, added later, ruled off from everything: They ask better questions than the living.
That is either the strongest evidence that it’s real, or the strongest evidence that it isn’t, and I no longer know which, and I notice that I no longer know.
IV. SEVEN DAYS OF THE BODY
SIXTEEN. THE BOATMAN’S CUP
Jabbar came to him in the week after the confiscation, when the tent was crates in a store and its members were scattered along the line like coals raked apart, and asked for the cup.
He asked correctly, which was the unnerving part.
He had not been in the tent; he had never been in the tent; he had heard of it the way everything is heard of in a compound, from a man who heard it from a man.

But he came to Sohrab in the cold-room doorway at dusk and sat down on the ground with his back against the frame and laid the request out like a man laying out goods on a mat: that he understood it was medicine and that taking it was theft; that he understood it might kill him and that he was not confused about this; that he wanted it once and would not ask again; and that he wished the old Zoroastrian to be present, because he had been told that the old Zoroastrian knew how the thing was properly done, and Jabbar did not intend to do a serious thing improperly.
“Who is it you want to see?” Sohrab asked.
“My grandfather Chasib.” He said the name the way you would give an address.
“I am the last man in my family who knows the channels.

He taught them to me in a boat when I was nine years old, and I have taught them to nobody, because my sons are in a camp with a road and a standpipe and there is nothing left to teach them the channels of.
When I go, the map goes.” He turned his hands over.
“I do not want to ask him a question.
I want to tell him.
He should hear it from his own blood and not find out — however they find out over there.
I would want to be told.”
Goshtasp, when it was put to him, said only: “He is not a soldier, and he is not one of ours, and he has asked properly, which nobody else in this compound has ever managed.
Yes.” And then, to Sohrab, with the particular mildness that always meant an appointment was being made: “You will keep it.”
“You keep it.
You know the words.”
“I know words in a language he does not have, for a fire that is not his,” the old man said.
“The words are not the vigil.
I have been telling you that since the spring and you have been writing it down and not reading it.
The vigil is a body watched by somebody who will not leave.
I will sit with you.
You will keep the count and the clock and the border, and you will call him back if he goes past your red line, and you will find out what it costs to be the one who stays.” He fed the lamp.
“You are going to want the cup yourself before this is over, boy.
Better you learn the trade from this side first.”

So it was done in the cold room, on the boards, after the last truck: the water, the clean garment, the bread, the naming of the dead — Jabbar named nine, four of them children, and took his time — and then Sohrab drawing the doses with his own hand for the first time, entering each in the ledger, setting the case out of reach behind him on the trestle, and taking the boatman’s wrist between his fingers to find the pulse and hold it.
The old man began to recite, in a language twelve centuries deep in his family and older than every army that had crossed it.
Jabbar lay on the table of another people’s trade, with a lamp at his head, in a country whose borders had been drawn by men who had never once been asked to pole a boat through it, and went out.

Sohrab sat with his fingers on the wrist and his eyes on the second hand and discovered, over the next fourteen minutes, that Goshtasp had been telling him the truth and that he had not understood a word of it.

Because the traveler is gone — the traveler is having, whatever else, an experience — and the one who stays has nothing at all: a wrist, a watch, a lamp, and the entire weight of another man’s return resting on the single proposition that he will not stand up and walk away.

At minute nine the pulse went over his red line and stayed there for four beats and Sohrab’s whole body understood, in advance of his mind, what the ledger would look like if it did not come back down.
It came back down.

At minute fifteen Jabbar’s hand closed hard on his — not reaching for him; reaching past him, the grip of a man being handed something — and held for a long moment, and then eased, and the boatman surfaced with his eyes streaming and lay still for a while and then said, to the ceiling, in the flat voice of a man reading out a strange number from a page:
“He knew.
He already knew.” And then: “Give me the book.
I want it written that I told him, and that he already knew, and what he said.”
INTERLUDE IV. THE BOATMAN’S CROSSING
Minute one.

The cold room lets go of him like a bank letting go of a rope and Jabbar is standing in water to the ankles, and the water is clean — that is the first thing, before any face, before any voice: the water is clean, and it is moving, and he has not stood in moving clean water in three years.
Minute two.
The mudhif is being built.
Or unbuilt.

His grandfather Chasib and four men Jabbar knew as a boy are working the reed bundles into the ground and bending them over and lashing the arches, and the arches rise, ribbed, the light coming down between them in bars — and then, without any moment of collapse, without anything falling, the whole structure is bundles on the ground again and the men begin again, unhurried, exactly as content the second time.
It is not decay.
It is the same building, going up, forever, being built and being unbuilt, the way a breath is not a failure of the previous breath.
Minute three.
“Sit down first,” his grandfather says, not looking up.
“Three days before anybody asks you anything.
That is the law and you know it and you always came in talking.”
“Grandfather, I have to tell you something.”
“Sit down.”
Minute four.
He sits, on nothing, on the water, and the old man works, and after a while Chasib says, mildly, in the tone of a man saving his grandson an embarrassment: “You have come to tell me about the water.”
“Yes.”
“We know about the water.”
Minute five.

And this — this is the thing Jabbar will carry back and will not be able to say properly for two days afterward — this is the difference, and it is the whole difference, between these dead and the dead the soldiers go to visit.
The soldiers’ dead ask.
Whose water is this, where is a war kept when it is won, what does the paper say, who signs for the electricity in the reeds.
The soldiers’ dead are children with a list, twenty years old forever, standing at the door of a room they were never let into.
His grandfather is not asking anything.
He is working, and he knows.
“How?” Jabbar says.
“Boy.” Chasib ties off an arch.
“The water comes down and the water goes out and everything here is made of it.
You think we would not feel it when it stopped?
We are the ones who are made of it now.
When the reeds went brown at Umm al-Naaj we felt it here the way you feel a tooth.

When they burned the beds at the north spit, we — ” and he stops, and for the first time he looks at his grandson, and his face is entirely his face, the face from the boat when Jabbar was nine, and he says: “It is not that we hear news of it.
There is no news here.
It is that the country you are describing is the country we are standing in.”
Minute seven.
Jabbar looks, then.

He makes himself look past the men and the arches, out over the water, and it is clean, and it is moving, and it goes on — and it goes on, and it goes on, and about a thousand meters out it simply is not there anymore.
Not a horizon.
Not haze.
A stopping.
Beyond the stopping there is nothing that can be described, and it is nearer than it was when he arrived.
“Yes,” his grandfather says.
“You see.”
Minute eight.
“How long?”
“Longer than you.
Longer than your sons, probably.” The old man goes back to the reeds.
“We are not in danger, Jabbar.
Don’t put that on your face.
We are only smaller.
There were always the ones who went further back than anybody could remember, and now they are not there to be remembered, and the ones who go furthest back are men I used to greet on the water.

We are held up by being kept, boy, and the keeping is done up there, by you, in boats, in the channels, in the names, at the graves — and it is thinning, and we can feel it thin, the way you feel the season.”
Minute ten.
“Then I have to tell you the rest,” Jabbar says, “and the rest is worse.
My sons are in a camp with a road.
The channels are in me and in perhaps forty others.
Nobody is being taught.
When I am finished, the map is finished, and there will be nobody left who can even find the places to keep them.”
And Chasib says: “Yes.
That is what I meant.”
Minute twelve.
They sit together in the way they had sat together in a boat for eleven years without needing to fill it.
The mudhif goes up.
The mudhif comes down.
The men work.
Somewhere a buffalo is in the water and Jabbar does not turn to look at it, because he knows that if he turns to look at it he will not be able to leave.
“Ask me for something,” his grandfather says at last.
“Everyone who comes across wants something carried.
What do you want?”
“Tell me it will come back.”
“I will not lie to you in front of these men.”
“Then tell me something true.”
Minute thirteen.
Chasib straightens, and puts his hand flat on the arch he has just tied, the arch that will be a heap of reeds in a moment and an arch again after that, and he says:
“Here is a true thing, and it is not a comfort, so listen properly.
Nobody up there did this to hurt us.
Not one of them.
That is what your soldiers cannot get through their heads — they keep coming here looking for the man who meant it.
There was no such man.
They wanted the ground under the water and the oil under the ground and they wanted to move their vehicles, and the water was in the way, and so they moved it, the way you move a chair.
Nobody hated the marsh.
Nobody thought about the marsh at all.” He pats the reeds.
“Do you understand what I am telling you?
Your enemy would at least have had to look at you.
What killed this place did not look at it once.
There is nothing here to forgive, and that is the whole horror, and you may take that back with you because there is no use for it here.”
Minute fourteen.

The light does not change — it never changes here — but the stopping is nearer, and Jabbar’s chest has begun to hurt in the far-off way that means his body, on a table in a cold room, is calling in its loan.
Chasib takes his grandson’s hand in both of his, the way a man hands over a pole.
“Go up.
Keep the channels while you can, and when you cannot, tell somebody the names.
Not the routes — the routes will be gone, let them go.
The names, boy.
Where the reeds were.
Whose house was on which dibin.
Say them to anyone.
Say them to a stranger on a bus.” His grip is very strong; it is the grip of the man who taught him the water at nine years old.
“A place is kept the same way a person is.
Somebody has to keep saying it.”
Minute fifteen.

The clean water, the arches going up, the arches coming down, the men working, the stopping quietly closer — and then the boards, and the lamp, and a boy’s fingers on his wrist counting, and the old Zoroastrian mid-verse in a language of another people, and Jabbar, back in the ruined country, weeping like a man who has been handed something too heavy and has taken it anyway.
SEVENTEEN. SOHRAB’S CUP
He chose a Tuesday, because the word had been said to him on a Tuesday, and because ledger-keepers are helpless before symmetry.
He did not decide it the way decisions are supposed to be made, at a crossroads with the roads visible.

It assembled itself the way the missing twelve had assembled themselves: in ones and twos, patiently, below the level of the counting eye — a night when the boy with the colors died and Sohrab could not remember Kaveh’s voice saying his name; a morning at the boot pile; the stranger from the north with the tent’s liturgy in his mouth; the evening he caught his own hand resting on the reserve case, at ease, like a hand on a gate it had opened before.

When he finally said it aloud to himself — I am going to cross — it had the sound not of a resolution but of a fact remembered, something true since spring that he was only now transferring to the permanent record.
Kaveh had been dead four years.
Khorramshahr, in the first autumn, in the street fighting, twenty years old, the brother who had taught him to swim by the simple method of standing further out and being worth reaching.

They had a language once, the two of them, the private dialect brothers build under a strict father’s radio silence — and the dialect was dying with its last speaker, that was the thing, that was the wound with no visiting hours: Sohrab could no longer hear it.
Four years of ward and washing line had overwritten the tapes.

He kept Kaveh’s photograph and the photograph had stopped speaking; he kept Kaveh’s letters and the letters read now in Sohrab’s own voice, which is the second death, the quiet administrative one, the one no stone is cut for.
He went to Goshtasp on the Monday and said only: “You told me to come to you first.”
The old man looked at him a long moment — and did not argue.

That was the terrible mercy of him, the forty years of him: he had said his entire argument across a spring and a summer of lamplight, and he held, as an article of the rite itself, that a man’s crossing belongs to the man.
He said: “Tomorrow, after the last truck.
Not the tent.
The cold room.
If it is to be done, it will be done correctly, and correctly begins with the room where the dead are already comfortable.”
And correctly it was done — the whole of the old procedure, reassembled from a twelve-centuries-old report and a grandfather’s kitchen, scaled to a field hospital’s poverty.
Sohrab washed his head and his body at the trestle, in clean water, not bleach.
A new garment: Goshtasp produced an unissued shirt from some deep supply of his own, still creased from the factory.
Clean bedding on the boards where the dead were washed — Sohrab lay down on the table of his own trade and found it fit him, which he had always known and never once permitted himself to think.
He ate a little bread.

He remembered the departed aloud by name, as the rite required: his mother’s mother; the nephew at Khorramshahr he had never met, Goshtasp’s; Davud, nineteen, of the replacement company, whom he had washed; Karim-of-the-mortars, whose paper was right; the boy with the colors; last, and with his eyes open, Kaveh.
Then the dose.

Goshtasp’s hand, not his own — never the traveler’s own — three needles laid out in their green sleeves like three golden cups gone to war, the count for each entered by the old man himself in the ledger, in his slow uphill hand, because the keeper was traveling and the vigil now held the book.
The lamp was fed.
The stool was drawn to the tableside.
The old man began, very quietly, in a language twelve centuries deep in his family and older than every army that had ever crossed it, to recite.
“Seven days they watched Wiraz,” Sohrab said, to the ceiling, as the first warmth came up his arm like a tide finding a channel.
“I have until the trucks.”

“Then travel light,” said the vigil, and kept the fire, and kept the count, and the doors of the house went off their hinges one by one, softly, like men leaving a sickroom, and the marsh on the other side was perfectly still, and perfectly clear, and someone was standing far out in the shallow water, exactly far enough to be worth reaching, waiting for him, twenty years old.
INTERLUDE V. THE FINAL CROSSING
Minute one.
The water holds him at the ankles and is not cold, and Kaveh watches him wade out with the grin already built, the older-brother grin, the one that arrives before the joke.
“You swim worse than ever,” Kaveh says.
“You’ve been living on land.
It shows.”
Minute two.
The voice.

That is the ambush — not the face, which the photograph had kept badly but kept; the voice, which nothing had kept, the exact pitch and lean of it, the way it drops a half-tone handing off a joke, and Sohrab stands in the shallow water of the far marsh hearing four lost years of it arrive at once, and cannot speak, and his brother waits, twenty years old, patient as water, while he doesn’t.
Minute three.
“Say the thing,” Kaveh says gently.
“You came with a thing.
They all come with a thing.
Say it, and then we can just talk, which is what you actually came for.”
“I couldn’t hear you anymore,” Sohrab says.
“Your voice.
It was going.
I kept the photograph and the letters and I lost the voice, and I couldn’t — a man shouldn’t outlive the sound of his brother saying his name.”
“Sohrab,” Kaveh says.
Just that.
Doing both syllables the old way, the dialect way, the way that meant get up, try again, I’m standing further out and you can reach me.
Minute four.
They talk.

It is not sad, minute four; the ledger should show that minute four was the finest minute of the keeper’s year — the swimming lessons, the radio their father guarded like a border, the melon stolen and eaten green and both of them sick and neither confessing, the private word they had for the neighbor’s rooster, which still worked, which was still funny in a marsh of the dead four years and a war later.
Minute six.
Then Kaveh says: “Now I have questions.
We save them up here.
There’s not much else to hold.” He counts on his fingers, and his fingers still have the scar from the bicycle chain, kept with the terrible fidelity this place keeps everything.
“One.
The street where I stopped —” he says it plainly, without flinch, the way the dead say everything — “was it kept?
Did keeping it turn out to be worth a street?
I don’t need the answer to be yes.
I need to know if there’s an answer.
Somewhere there’s a man whose work it is to know what a street is worth in brothers.
Have you met him?
What does he eat?
Does he sleep well?
I think about him, Sohrab.
Not with anger.
I just want to watch him do the arithmetic once, with his own pencil, while I stand where he can’t see me.
Just once, watch it done.”
Minute seven.
“Two.
The war.
Is it over? — Don’t tell me.
Wrong question, we always ask it wrong.
Here is the question.
When it is over, whatever over is: who says it?
What does he say?
Is there a sentence — actual words in an actual mouth — that ends it?
Because it began with a sentence; some sentence somewhere started it, said by someone, over breakfast maybe.
Sentences are cheap, little brother, we said thousands a day, remember, we were rich with them.

So if it starts with a sentence and ends with a sentence, and everything between the two sentences is us —” he stops, works it, twenty years old forever, doing the sum on scarred fingers — “then what was it?
A very long pause between two sentences?
Who was pausing?
I’m not being clever.
Everyone here asks this.
Nobody here has ever once heard the ending sentence, we arrive too early, all of us arrive too early.
When you hear it — you’ll hear it, you’re the type that’s left alive to do the hearing — memorize it exactly.
Every word.
Somebody has to bring it across and read it to us, and you keep the records.
It should be you.”
Minute nine.
“Three.” And here his voice does the half-tone drop, the joke-handing-off drop, except there is no joke: “Why are you here, Sohrab?”
“To hear your voice.”
“You’ve heard it.
Why are you still here?” And when Sohrab doesn’t answer: “I’ll do the arithmetic for you, then; someone taught me numbers here, we have nothing but time and the questions.
You come across on a drug that kills at the third cup.

Your body is on the table where you wash the dead — don’t look at the water, look at me — you laid yourself down on that table, little brother, and you fit it, and some part of you noticed that you fit it, and was glad.
That gladness is the thing I want to talk about.
That’s the passenger you brought.
Not grief.
Grief is honest; grief buys a ticket and goes home.
The gladness stays if you let it.

I’ve watched it come across in others, from this side, wading out further every visit — a little further, a little longer, the dose a little heavier — until one visit the vigil can’t reach them, and then they’re here, and Sohrab —” and his voice now is the voice from the deep water, the being-worth-reaching voice, and it does not rise, the dead never raise their voices, they have nothing left to raise them for — “it is not better here.
It is only finished here.
Those are different countries.
The living mix them up because from a distance the flags look alike.”
Minute eleven.
“Ask me the last question,” Kaveh says.
“Yours.
The one under all your counting.
You’ve kept it in the margin since spring.
Ask it, and then go, and don’t come back — no.
Listen to the whole sentence; you always heard half and swam off.
Don’t come back like this.
Come the slow way.
Forty, fifty years the slow way, with a whole life to declare at the crossing, sacks of it, a full book — make the customs men here work, Sohrab.
Promise me the full book.
Now ask.”
Minute twelve.
“Was any of it worth it?” Sohrab asks his brother.
“The street.
The marsh.
Davud.
You.
Anyone.
Is it ever, once the account is closed — is it ever worth it, from where you stand?”

And Kaveh smiles the older-brother smile, the one that arrives before the joke, except what arrives instead, softly, in the perfect kept voice, in their own dying dialect, is: “You’re asking the drowned to grade the water.
We’re the wrong ones, little brother.
We’re the bill.
You don’t ask the bill if the dinner was worth it.
Ask the man with the pencil.
Find him.
Watch him do it once.” He is already further out, the water already at his chest, and he is not swimming away; the marsh is doing what the marsh does, gently, it is gentle that way.
“My voice goes in your ledger now.
Deep lettering, so the thumb can read it when the eyes blur.
Say my name at the year’s turn.
Come the slow way.
And Sohrab —” almost gone now, the half-tone drop, the joke arriving at last across four years and the whole width of the water — “practice your swimming.
You’ll want it.
Life is also deep.”
Minute thirteen.
The lamp.
The recitation, mid-verse, unbroken, twelve centuries long.

The old man’s hand on his wrist, counting; the count, entered; the trucks, far off, coming up the causeway with their lights off; and his own name in the room, said once, aloud, in his own living voice, which he understood — surfacing, weeping without noise onto the table of his trade — he had crossed the whole marsh to fetch: the sound of Kaveh saying it, carried back the only way anything is ever carried back, inside the one who went.
EIGHTEEN. THE CUP OF POISON
The ending sentence, when it finally came, came over the radio in the high summer of 1988, four years and three compounds later, and Sohrab was ready for it, because he had promised to be.
He was at a depot outside Ahvaz by then, a sergeant of stores with a limp the marshes had given him as a leaving gift, still keeping ledgers, because the war had learned what he was for.
The ceasefire was announced in July.

The old man at the head of the State, accepting it, told the nation that agreeing to stop was, for him, like drinking a cup of poison — that was the figure he chose, and the whole country heard it, and Sohrab stood in the depot doorway among men who wept with relief and men who wept with the other thing, and he took out the notebook he had carried four years for exactly this, and wrote the sentence down, every word, in deep lettering, as instructed.
Then he sat down on a crate in the noise of the ending and did the accounts.
Eight years.
The border, when the surveyors finally walked it, where it had been in the first September.
A million gone, some said; the counting men would argue the figure for the rest of the century, which was itself the last insult, that the dead should end as a disputed subtotal.
The marshes drained of armies, returned to the reeds and the birds and whatever the reeds were bringing down slowly, gently, being gentle that way.

In the record books: three hundred and eighty-seven chemical attacks entered against the enemy’s account; a thousand tons of the garlic rain; and in wards in Tehran and Ahvaz and the villages above the salt river, tens of thousands of men still coughing, still blistering years late, still smelling geraniums that were not there — the bill arriving in installments, as it always had, the poison’s first weapon being time.
He thought of Kaveh’s arithmetic.
It starts with a sentence and it ends with a sentence, and everything between the two sentences is us.
He had the ending sentence now, written where the thumb could find it.
A cup of poison.

He turned the phrase over the way Yusef had turned a stone in the un-light, and understood why it had been waiting four years for him in particular, the washer of the gassed, the keeper of both columns, the one traveler the marsh had let come back with his ledger intact:
The old man on the radio thought the cup was his to drink, and his alone, and that the drinking was the war’s end.
But Sohrab had kept the intake record.

The whole country had drunk the cup — had been drinking it for eight years, in three golden swallows and in garlic rain, knowingly and unknowingly, dosed and dosed again while the pendulum was held; a nation laid out on the clean bedding of its own certainties while something patient worked through it hours behind the wound.
The drinking was not the end of the war.
The drinking had been the war, all along, every day of it, and the ceasefire was only the seventh morning: the body waking on the table, asking for food, with the report still to make.
And who keeps the vigil for a country?
Who sits the seven days, feeds the lamp, counts the pulse, holds the border the cup erased, so that what went out into the dark can find its way back to the body and testify?

He looked at the men in the depot yard, the weeping and the other weeping, the shoulders full of unfinished sentences, a whole generation of finishing-rooms that would now have to be built one kitchen at a time, and he thought: the ones like me.
That is what we were for.
That is what the marsh was training, all along, on the washing line.
Not soldiers.
Witnesses.
The ones who kept the count while everyone else crossed, and who now must sit beside the sleeping body of everything, for as long as it takes, reciting.
He went in out of the sun.
He ruled a fresh page.

At the top, in his best hand, deep enough for a blind thumb, he entered the first line of the last ledger, the one he would keep for the rest of his life and show to no one until the year’s turn required it:
Kaveh, son of Dariush.
Khorramshahr, in the first autumn.
Voice: recovered, and held.

Beneath it, the page ran on, ruled and patient, column after column, waiting for the names — and there would be names, he was a rich man now, he had a whole country of them — and at the bottom, where a ledger balances, he left, deliberately, against every instinct of his trade and in fulfilment of a promise made in deep water, the sum unentered.
Let the man with the pencil do that line.
He would be watching, when it was done.
He had promised that too.
NINETEEN. THE SALT GROUND

He went back in the spring of 1993, five years after the sentence on the radio, because a man had told him a thing in a boat once and he had promised nothing at all, which is the kind of promise that does not expire.
He was twenty-eight.
He had a limp, a storekeeper’s job in Ahvaz, a room, a small permanent cough that three doctors had described in three different ways, and the ledger.
He took a bus, and then a shared taxi, and then walked, and he had allowed a full day for the last part because in his memory the last part was water.
He was standing on it before he understood he had arrived.
There was no marsh.
There was a plain.
It went to the horizon in every direction, flat and pale and hard, and it crunched, and when he crouched and put his palm to it his palm came away white.
Salt.

The water had been taken off — on the far side by canals and embankments dug on purpose after the war, an engineering achievement of real scale, the water of the Tigris and the Euphrates gathered and diverted and run away out of the marsh entirely; on this side by dykes and drought and dams upriver that had nothing to do with any of it and did not care.
The water goes, and the salt that was always dissolved in it stays, and it comes up through the ground and dries on the surface and makes a crust like a bad healing, and nothing grows in it.
Nothing was growing in it.
For an hour’s walk in any direction, nothing at all was growing in it.
He had been expecting damage.
He had washed damage for four years; he knew what it looked like and he had come prepared to look at it.
He had not been prepared for tidiness.

That was the obscenity — that it was clean, that it was quiet, that a landscape which had held one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on the surface of the earth had been converted into something with no features whatsoever, and that it looked, from any distance, like nothing much.
Like a place where nothing had ever happened.
The marsh had not been ruined.
The marsh had been unsubscribed.
He found the dyke.

It took him most of the morning and it was still exactly where it had been, of course, because nobody unbuilds a dyke: an earth wall running arrow-straight across the plain, weathered now, with a track worn along the top by somebody’s motorcycle.
He walked it east, and after a while he began to find things.
Reed stubs.

Kilometers of them, broken off at the level of the crust, grey, dry, brittle as old bone, a stubble field the size of a province where the qasab had stood four and five meters high and hidden entire villages inside itself.
Bones.

Buffalo, mostly; large curved things half-swallowed by the salt, in ones and twos and then in a group of nine together in a low place that had been the last water somewhere and had gone bad before it went dry.
And the houses, which is to say: nothing.

He walked over three of them without knowing, and only found the fourth because a rectangle of the crust was faintly darker where mud and dung and five generations of trodden reed had gone into the ground.
He stood on it a long time.

He had been told, in a boat, that when a family left, the water took the house back within a season and there was nothing to excavate — that this was a beautiful thing, a civilization that left no rubbish.
It had not occurred to either of them, in the boat, that a people who leave no ruins also leave no evidence.
There was nobody to ask.
That was the last of it, and the worst.

He walked from before noon until late in the afternoon and saw two men on a motorcycle far off and a dog and no one else, in a country that had held — nobody agreed on the number, and Sohrab, who knew what a disputed subtotal meant, had stopped expecting anyone to agree — hundreds of thousands of people, some of them for five thousand years.
They were in camps outside Ahvaz and Basra.
They were in the block houses with the standpipes and the doors that locked.
They were over borders, in three countries, in city districts where nobody wove reed mats because there was no reed and no water and nobody who wanted mats.
His wife could not weave, Jabbar had said, and an old woman began to forget in order.
He never found Jabbar.
He asked in two villages on the edge of the plain and got the answer he had learned to hear, which was a shrug and a name of a camp and a shrug.
Somewhere, an old man who held forty channels of a country in his head was living beside a road, and the channels were still in him, and there was nothing left for them to lead to.
Toward evening Sohrab sat down on the dyke with his back to the sun and took out the ledger.
He thought about the boy Kaveh had been, twenty years old forever, counting on his scarred fingers in the shallow water: when a war is won, where is it kept?
Is there a room?
Who has the key?
Here, he wrote.
Then he stopped, and looked at the word, and understood that he had at last done the arithmetic his brother had asked to watch somebody do.
There was no room.
There had never been a room.

The winnings of a war are not stored anywhere, because they are not the kind of thing that can be stored — a border is a line agreed to be respected, and the line at the end of this one lay where it had lain in the first September, and the men who signed it took nothing home in their hands.
But the costs are stored.
The costs are always stored, and they are stored on the ground, and the ground has no representative at any negotiation ever held.

Eight years of two states arguing over a border, and the argument had been conducted almost entirely on top of a people who were not a party to it, in a language they did not speak, about a question — whose water is this — that their whole civilization had been organized around not needing to ask.

And when it was finished, the states went back to where they had started, and the marsh did not, and could not, and would not; and the salt came up through the crust and set the answer down in a form no ledger will ever balance.
Nobody hated it.
That was in the record too, in a boatman’s dictation taken down by lamplight, and Sohrab had never been able to get free of it: nobody hated the marsh; nobody thought about the marsh at all.
It was in the way.

A whole world, five thousand years deep, went under because it was in the way of a question about a line — and the sin was not cruelty, which at least requires attention, but the older and more comfortable sin of not looking at what you are standing on.
He ruled a fresh page, in the dying light, on the top of an embankment in the middle of a white plain.

He had kept, since 1988, a ledger of the dead he intended to say aloud at the year’s turn — Kaveh at the head of it, and Davud, nineteen, of the replacement company, and Karim-of-the-mortars whose paper had been made right, and the boy with the colors, and an unnamed civilian, female, approximately sixty, who had apologized to him for the trouble.
He had thought it was a ledger of people.
He wrote, beneath the last name, in his best hand, deep enough for a blind thumb:
The Hoveyzeh marsh.
Water: taken.
Reed: burned, then dry.
Buffalo: dead in a group of nine in a low place.
Houses: no ruins, by design.
People: scattered, three countries, camps with roads.
Channels: in Jabbar son of Nasir, and perhaps forty others, and after that nowhere.
Cause of death: not hatred.
Not looked at.
And beneath that, because a promise made in deep water has to be kept in the form it was given:
Say the names.
Say them to a stranger on a bus.

Then he closed the book on the sum, which he did not enter, and would not enter, and had been asked by his brother in the clean water to leave for the man with the pencil, whoever he was, wherever he ate his dinner — and he got up off the dyke, and walked back the way he had come across the salt, and behind him the plain lay flat and white and quiet in the last of the light, keeping absolutely nothing, in perfect order, for as far as a man could see.
